Bhagavad Gita 2.71.keyIdea: Letting go of wanting, owning, and ego brings inner peace.
Bhagavad Gita 2.71.contextNote: The verse describes a state of mind—not a rule about what you must do, but what happens when someone stops grasping and claiming.

Bhagavad Gita 2.70.simpleEnglish: When desires come to someone, they flow in like rivers into the ocean. The ocean stays calm and in one place even when water keeps filling it. A person who lets desires come and go without chasing them finds peace. But someone who keeps wanting more things will not find peace.
Bhagavad Gita 2.70.keyIdea: Peace comes from letting desires pass through you without clinging to them, not from chasing every desire.
Bhagavad Gita 2.70.contextNote: The verse uses the ocean as a picture: it receives water from all directions but stays steady and unmoved. A calm mind works the same way.

Bhagavad Gita 2.72.simpleEnglish: This is the state of Brahmic steadiness, Arjuna (the warrior Krishna is teaching). When you reach it, confusion leaves you. Even at the moment of death, if you are in this state, you attain brahma-nirvana—the bliss of Brahman (the ultimate reality).
Bhagavad Gita 2.72.keyIdea: A steady, clear mind rooted in Brahman brings freedom from delusion and peace even at death.
Bhagavad Gita 2.72.contextNote: This verse concludes Krishna's teaching on the two paths of action and knowledge. It describes the final fruit of the Brahmic state—a mind so stable that it remains undisturbed even when life ends.

Bhagavad Gita 3.1.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior) asks Krishna: "You say that devotion is better than action. So why are you telling me to fight this terrible battle?"
Bhagavad Gita 3.1.keyIdea: Arjuna is confused because Krishna seems to value devotion over action, yet is pushing him toward war.
Bhagavad Gita 3.1.contextNote: This is Arjuna's opening question in the Gita. He is troubled by the command to fight and wants to understand why Krishna values devotion if action is what matters now.

Bhagavad Gita 3.2.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) tells Krishna that his words are confusing and mixed up. He asks Krishna to tell him one clear thing: what is the best path for him to follow?
Bhagavad Gita 3.2.keyIdea: Arjuna asks Krishna to stop being unclear and give him one straight answer about what he should do.
Bhagavad Gita 3.2.contextNote: Arjuna is frustrated because Krishna has been giving him different ideas about duty and action. Arjuna wants a simple, definite answer.

Bhagavad Gita 3.4.simpleEnglish: You cannot reach freedom just by doing nothing. You also cannot reach perfection just by giving things up. Both action and renunciation matter.
Bhagavad Gita 3.4.keyIdea: Freedom and perfection require more than passivity or withdrawal alone.
Bhagavad Gita 3.4.contextNote: This verse responds to a common misunderstanding: that spiritual progress comes from either avoiding all work or abandoning all possessions. Krishna is saying neither extreme works by itself.

Bhagavad Gita 3.3.simpleEnglish: Krishna says there are two paths people follow in this world. One path is for those who study and think deeply about truth—they reach it through knowledge. The other path is for those who act and serve—they reach it through work.
Bhagavad Gita 3.3.keyIdea: Two different ways lead to the same goal: understanding through study, or understanding through action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.3.contextNote: This verse introduces a main theme of the Gita: that different people may find their way through different methods, but both are valid.

Bhagavad Gita 3.5.simpleEnglish: No one can stay still, not even for a moment. Everyone has to do something. The qualities of nature (the three gunas—sattva, rajas, and tamas) push all living beings to act, whether they want to or not.
Bhagavad Gita 3.5.keyIdea: All beings are constantly driven to action by the forces of nature within them.
Bhagavad Gita 3.5.contextNote: This verse introduces a key teaching: action is not optional. Even trying to do nothing is itself an action, and the natural qualities that make up all living things compel movement and work.

Bhagavad Gita 3.8.simpleEnglish: Do your duty. Action is better than doing nothing. You cannot even keep your body alive without doing something.
Bhagavad Gita 3.8.keyIdea: Doing your duty is better than inaction, because even basic survival requires action.

Bhagavad Gita 3.6.simpleEnglish: Someone who holds back their hands and body from acting on desires, but keeps thinking about those desires in their mind, is not being honest. That person is called a hypocrite.
Bhagavad Gita 3.6.keyIdea: Pretending to control yourself while secretly wanting the same things is dishonest.
Bhagavad Gita 3.6.contextNote: The verse is about the gap between what you do and what you really want. It says that kind of split is a form of lying.

Bhagavad Gita 3.7.simpleEnglish: Someone who controls their senses with their mind, stays free from attachment, and does their work with full attention—that person is far superior. Krishna is telling Arjuna that this kind of discipline and focus matters more than avoiding action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.7.keyIdea: Controlling your senses and doing your duty without attachment is better than trying to escape from action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.7.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has explained that action itself is not wrong—it is attachment and desire that cause problems. Here he shows what a person looks like when they act the right way.

Bhagavad Gita 3.10.simpleEnglish: Long ago, the Creator made people and gave them sacrifice (a ritual practice). The Creator said, "Use this sacrifice. It will give you what you need."
Bhagavad Gita 3.10.keyIdea: The Creator connected people to sacrifice as a way to receive what they need.
Bhagavad Gita 3.10.contextNote: This verse explains an old teaching: sacrifice is a tool for getting results. It sets up an idea Krishna will explore in the chapter.

Bhagavad Gita 3.9.simpleEnglish: The world gets trapped when people act for their own sake. But action done for sacrifice (a gift or offering to something beyond yourself) does not trap the world. So Arjuna, do your work without clinging to what you gain from it.
Bhagavad Gita 3.9.keyIdea: Work done with attachment to its rewards binds people; work done as an offering frees them.
Bhagavad Gita 3.9.contextNote: Krishna is teaching Arjuna about the difference between selfish action and action offered up. "Sacrifice" here means dedicating your work to something larger than yourself, not just personal gain.

Bhagavad Gita 3.11.simpleEnglish: Please the gods with this sacrifice, and the gods will please you in return. When you help each other this way, everyone reaches the highest good.
Bhagavad Gita 3.11.keyIdea: Mutual care—between humans and gods, and among people—leads to the best outcome.
Bhagavad Gita 3.11.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about sacrifice (yajna). The "gods" here are divine powers in Hindu thought, not separate beings in the modern sense. The idea is that when we give and receive in a cycle of care, everyone benefits.

Bhagavad Gita 3.12.simpleEnglish: When people make sacrifices (offerings to the gods), the gods give them good things in return. But if someone enjoys those good things without giving back to others, that person is stealing.
Bhagavad Gita 3.12.keyIdea: Taking a gift without giving back is like theft.
Bhagavad Gita 3.12.contextNote: This verse teaches about reciprocity—the idea that receiving creates an obligation to give. In the Gita's worldview, the gods and humans exchange gifts through sacrifice and generosity.

Bhagavad Gita 3.13.simpleEnglish: People who eat food left over from a sacrifice (a ritual offering) are freed from wrongdoing. But people who cook food only for themselves, without sharing, take on sin.
Bhagavad Gita 3.13.keyIdea: Sharing food from a sacrifice brings freedom from sin; cooking only for yourself brings sin.
Bhagavad Gita 3.13.contextNote: In this teaching, a "sacrifice" is a ritual act of offering. The verse contrasts two ways of eating: one tied to a shared ritual, one purely selfish.

Bhagavad Gita 3.14.simpleEnglish: All living things come from food. Food grows because of rain. Rain comes from sacrifices (rituals and offerings). Sacrifices happen because of action and work.
Bhagavad Gita 3.14.keyIdea: Everything in nature is connected: action leads to ritual, ritual brings rain, rain grows food, and food sustains all life.
Bhagavad Gita 3.14.contextNote: This verse describes a chain of cause and effect. In the Gita's worldview, human actions and rituals are woven into the natural cycle that keeps all creatures alive.

Bhagavad Gita 3.15.simpleEnglish: Action comes from the Vedas (the oldest Hindu scriptures). The Vedas come from something eternal and unchanging. So the Vedas, which reach everywhere, are always connected to sacrifice (ritual offerings).
Bhagavad Gita 3.15.keyIdea: The Vedas are the source of action and are rooted in something eternal.
Bhagavad Gita 3.15.contextNote: Krishna is explaining where action comes from and why the Vedas matter. He links action, scripture, and ritual as part of one system.

Bhagavad Gita 3.16.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (the son of Pritha) that if someone does not turn the wheel that is already rolling, they live a wasted life. This person gives in to their senses and acts in a way that brings harm.
Bhagavad Gita 3.16.keyIdea: Not participating in the natural cycle of action and duty leads to a wasted life.
Bhagavad Gita 3.16.contextNote: The "wheel" refers to the cycle of action and duty that Krishna has been describing. To "turn" it means to act in harmony with one's role and responsibilities.

Bhagavad Gita 3.17.simpleEnglish: A person who finds joy in their own self, is satisfied with their own self, and is pleased with their own self has no work to do. This verse describes someone who is completely content within themselves.
Bhagavad Gita 3.17.keyIdea: A person who is fully satisfied with themselves has no need for action or work.
Bhagavad Gita 3.17.contextNote: This verse appears in Krishna's teaching about action and duty. It describes a state of complete inner contentment, which is presented as a contrast to the active life of duty that Krishna is encouraging.

Bhagavad Gita 3.18.simpleEnglish: A person who has reached a certain spiritual state does not need anything from action or inaction. He does not depend on other beings for his wellbeing.
Bhagavad Gita 3.18.keyIdea: A spiritually advanced person is not dependent on the results of actions or on other beings.
Bhagavad Gita 3.18.contextNote: This verse describes someone who has moved beyond needing things from the world or from others—a state the Gita calls freedom from attachment.

Bhagavad Gita 3.19.simpleEnglish: Do the work you need to do, but do not cling to it or worry about what happens because of it. When a person acts this way—doing what must be done but staying free from attachment—they reach the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 3.19.keyIdea: Work done without clinging to results leads to the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 3.19.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of acting: do what is necessary, but do not hold tight to the outcome or let it control your mind.

Bhagavad Gita 3.21.simpleEnglish: When a great person does something, other people copy it. People follow the example that a leader sets.
Bhagavad Gita 3.21.keyIdea: Leaders shape how others behave by their own actions.
Bhagavad Gita 3.21.contextNote: This verse is about influence and example. It does not say whether the leader's example is good or bad—only that people tend to follow it.

Bhagavad Gita 3.22.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (son of Pritha) that he has no duties left to do in all the worlds, and nothing left to gain that he hasn't already gained. Yet he still acts and works.
Bhagavad Gita 3.22.keyIdea: A being who has everything and needs nothing can still choose to act.
Bhagavad Gita 3.22.contextNote: Krishna is explaining why he continues to work even though he lacks nothing. This sets up his teaching about acting without attachment to results.

Bhagavad Gita 3.20.simpleEnglish: Kings like Janaka (a wise ruler in old stories) reached perfection through their work and duties. Krishna tells Arjuna: you should act too, and think about how your actions help keep people steady in their own duties.
Bhagavad Gita 3.20.keyIdea: Even great leaders worked through action, not by sitting still—and your work matters for others too.
Bhagavad Gita 3.20.contextNote: Arjuna has been hesitating about fighting. Krishna points to examples of wise kings who acted and found perfection through their duties. The verse suggests that action itself, done rightly, is a path to growth.

Bhagavad Gita 3.23.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (the son of Pritha): if he ever stopped working hard and fell into laziness, people everywhere would copy him and do the same. When a leader acts, others watch and follow.
Bhagavad Gita 3.23.keyIdea: A leader's actions set an example that others will follow.
Bhagavad Gita 3.23.contextNote: Krishna is explaining why he keeps working even though he has no personal need to. He is saying that his example matters to the world.

Bhagavad Gita 3.24.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: if I stopped doing my duty, these worlds would fall apart. I would cause confusion in the social order, and I would harm all these people.
Bhagavad Gita 3.24.keyIdea: A leader's duty matters because others depend on it.
Bhagavad Gita 3.24.contextNote: Krishna is explaining why he must act, even though he is divine. He is saying that duty and action are necessary to keep things in order.

Bhagavad Gita 3.25.simpleEnglish: Ignorant people do their work with attachment—they want the results for themselves. A wise person does the same work without attachment, not wanting anything for themselves. They do it to help keep people on the right path.
Bhagavad Gita 3.25.keyIdea: A wise person acts without selfish desire, but still does their duty to help others.
Bhagavad Gita 3.25.contextNote: This verse contrasts two ways of working: one driven by personal desire, the other by duty to others. The wise person's work looks the same on the outside, but comes from a different inner state.

Bhagavad Gita 3.26.simpleEnglish: A wise person should not confuse people who are still learning and who care deeply about their work. Instead, the wise person should do their own work with full attention and devotion, and show others by example how to do all their work well.
Bhagavad Gita 3.26.keyIdea: A wise teacher leads by example, not by shaking the beliefs of those still on their path.
Bhagavad Gita 3.26.contextNote: Krishna is telling Arjuna how a wise person should act toward others. The idea is about teaching through example rather than argument.

Bhagavad Gita 3.27.simpleEnglish: A person who is confused by ego thinks "I am doing this action." But really, the qualities of nature (like strength, passion, and dullness) are what make things happen. The person is not the real doer.
Bhagavad Gita 3.27.keyIdea: Ego makes us think we control our actions, but nature's qualities are actually at work.
Bhagavad Gita 3.27.contextNote: This verse describes a common mistake: believing "I am the one acting" when really our nature and circumstances shape what we do.

Bhagavad Gita 3.28.simpleEnglish: A person who understands how qualities (like anger, kindness, or laziness) work and how actions come from those qualities does not get attached to what happens. They see that qualities are just acting on other qualities—like one force pushing against another.
Bhagavad Gita 3.28.keyIdea: Understanding how qualities and actions work together can free you from attachment to results.
Bhagavad Gita 3.28.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of thinking: if you see that your actions and their results come from natural qualities at work, you can step back from feeling personally responsible or emotionally caught up in them.

Bhagavad Gita 3.29.simpleEnglish: People who don't understand how nature works get caught up in doing actions because of it. Someone who does understand should not try to shake the beliefs of people who don't yet understand.
Bhagavad Gita 3.29.keyIdea: A wise person should not force their understanding on those who are still learning.
Bhagavad Gita 3.29.contextNote: The verse speaks about two kinds of people: those confused by nature's qualities (guṇas), and those with complete knowledge. It teaches a lesson about how to treat others who see things differently.

Bhagavad Gita 3.30.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna to give all his actions to Krishna, with his mind understanding the connection between the highest self and his own self. Then fight the battle without wanting things for yourself, without thinking "this is mine," and without worry or fever in your heart.
Bhagavad Gita 3.30.keyIdea: Act with your whole heart, but give the results to Krishna and let go of desire and ownership.
Bhagavad Gita 3.30.contextNote: This verse teaches a way to act without being trapped by wanting rewards or fearing loss. The "fever" is a metaphor for the heat of anxiety and attachment.

Bhagavad Gita 3.31.simpleEnglish: People who follow this teaching steadily, with faith and without complaint, become free from the burden of their actions.
Bhagavad Gita 3.31.keyIdea: Following the teaching with faith and without doubt brings freedom from the weight of actions.
Bhagavad Gita 3.31.contextNote: This verse speaks about the result of living by Krishna's teaching. "Free from all actions" means the person is no longer trapped by the results of what they do.

Bhagavad Gita 3.32.simpleEnglish: People who complain about Krishna's teaching and do not follow it are confused. They lack good judgment and have lost their way.
Bhagavad Gita 3.32.keyIdea: Rejecting and ignoring wise teaching leads to confusion and poor judgment.
Bhagavad Gita 3.32.contextNote: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna about the consequences of dismissing his guidance. This verse appears in a section where Krishna explains the importance of following dharma (duty).

Bhagavad Gita 3.33.simpleEnglish: Even someone who knows a lot acts according to their own nature. All living things follow their nature. So what good does it do to hold back?
Bhagavad Gita 3.33.keyIdea: Knowledge alone does not change how a person naturally acts.
Bhagavad Gita 3.33.contextNote: Krishna is saying that understanding something intellectually is not the same as being able to control your natural tendencies. This verse appears in a discussion about action and desire.

Bhagavad Gita 3.34.simpleEnglish: Each sense—sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell—naturally likes some things and dislikes others. These likes and dislikes are built in. But you should not let them control you, because they work against you.
Bhagavad Gita 3.34.keyIdea: Our senses pull us toward what they like and away from what they dislike, and we can choose not to follow that pull.
Bhagavad Gita 3.34.contextNote: The verse is about the difference between having a preference and being ruled by it. The senses will always have their nature, but a person can learn not to be their slave.

Bhagavad Gita 3.35.simpleEnglish: It is better to do your own duty poorly than to do someone else's duty well. If you die doing your own duty, that is good. Doing someone else's duty brings danger.
Bhagavad Gita 3.35.keyIdea: Your own role in life, even if you do it imperfectly, is better than doing someone else's role well.
Bhagavad Gita 3.35.contextNote: This verse teaches about *dharma*—the duty or role that belongs to you. The idea is that each person has their own work to do, and it matters more to do that work than to do someone else's work, even if you could do theirs better.

Bhagavad Gita 3.36.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) asks Krishna: "Why does a person do wrong things even when they don't want to? It's as if something is forcing them to do it."
Bhagavad Gita 3.36.keyIdea: Arjuna is asking what makes people act against their own wishes and do harmful things.
Bhagavad Gita 3.36.contextNote: This is the start of Arjuna's question. He is puzzled about why people commit sin or do wrong even when they know it is wrong and don't want to.

Bhagavad Gita 3.37.simpleEnglish: The Deity describes desire and anger as enemies that grow from passion (one of the three qualities of nature). These forces are always hungry for more and lead to harm. They are the real enemy you face in life.
Bhagavad Gita 3.37.keyIdea: Desire and anger, born from passion, are destructive forces that work against you.
Bhagavad Gita 3.37.contextNote: This verse names desire and anger as a single enemy—they are linked. The "quality of passion" (rajas) is one of three fundamental forces in the world according to Hindu philosophy.

Bhagavad Gita 3.38.simpleEnglish: Fire gets hidden under smoke. A mirror gets covered with dust. A baby grows inside the womb. In the same way, desire covers up knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 3.38.keyIdea: Desire hides the truth, just as smoke hides fire or dust hides a mirror.
Bhagavad Gita 3.38.contextNote: Krishna is using three everyday examples to show how desire works—it doesn't destroy knowledge, but it covers it up so we can't see clearly.

Bhagavad Gita 3.39.simpleEnglish: Knowledge gets covered up by desire, which is always fighting against anyone who tries to know things. Desire is like a fire that never gets full—it always wants more.
Bhagavad Gita 3.39.keyIdea: Desire hides knowledge the way smoke hides a flame.
Bhagavad Gita 3.39.contextNote: Krishna is explaining why knowledge alone is not enough. Even when someone understands something true, wanting things can cloud that understanding and pull them away from it.

Bhagavad Gita 3.40.simpleEnglish: The senses, the mind, and understanding are where desire lives. Desire uses these to confuse a person and cover up their knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 3.40.keyIdea: Desire works through the senses and mind to hide a person's true understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 3.40.contextNote: This verse describes how desire (kama) operates—not as something outside us, but through our own faculties. It clouds judgment by blocking clear knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 3.42.simpleEnglish: The senses (like sight and hearing) are powerful. The mind is more powerful than the senses. Understanding is more powerful than the mind. And there is something even greater than understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 3.42.keyIdea: There is a hierarchy: senses, mind, understanding, and something beyond understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 3.42.contextNote: This verse lists levels of inner capacity, each one deeper or more controlling than the last. The final "that" is left unnamed here—the verse does not say what it is.

Bhagavad Gita 3.43.simpleEnglish: Now that you know what is higher than the mind, use your own strength to control yourself. Destroy this enemy that is hard to defeat—the desire that takes so many shapes.
Bhagavad Gita 3.43.keyIdea: Understanding something beyond the thinking mind gives you the power to master your own desires.
Bhagavad Gita 3.43.contextNote: Krishna is telling Arjuna that desire is an enemy because it keeps changing form and is difficult to overcome. But if you know what lies beyond ordinary thinking, you can use your own inner strength to defeat it.

Bhagavad Gita 3.41.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (a warrior of the Bharata line) to control his senses first. Then he should throw off this "sinful thing"—desire—which destroys both knowledge and wisdom. When desire runs wild, it blocks what a person can learn and understand.
Bhagavad Gita 3.41.keyIdea: Controlling the senses comes before you can overcome desire and keep your mind clear.
Bhagavad Gita 3.41.contextNote: This verse follows Krishna's teaching that desire and anger cloud judgment. He is telling Arjuna the practical step: master your senses so desire cannot pull you away from what is true.

Bhagavad Gita 4.1.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: "I taught this eternal teaching to Vivasvan (the sun god). Vivasvan taught it to Manu (an ancient king). Manu passed it on to Ikshvaku (his son, founder of a royal line)."
Bhagavad Gita 4.1.keyIdea: Krishna is explaining that this teaching has been passed down through a chain of teachers, starting from the beginning of time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.1.contextNote: This verse opens a new section where Krishna explains the history of the yoga (teaching) he is about to share. It establishes that what he teaches is ancient and has been transmitted carefully from teacher to student.

Bhagavad Gita 4.2.simpleEnglish: This teaching passed from teacher to student, and royal sages (wise kings) knew it. But over a very long time, it was lost and forgotten.
Bhagavad Gita 4.2.keyIdea: A spiritual teaching was once known but disappeared because so much time passed.
Bhagavad Gita 4.2.contextNote: Krishna is explaining why he is teaching Arjuna now—the knowledge had been lost to the world and needs to be shared again.

Bhagavad Gita 4.3.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that he is sharing an ancient teaching about devotion with him today. He does this because Arjuna is his devotee and friend. Krishna calls this teaching the highest mystery.
Bhagavad Gita 4.3.keyIdea: Krishna is about to teach Arjuna something sacred because of their relationship of devotion and friendship.
Bhagavad Gita 4.3.contextNote: This verse introduces Krishna's teaching. The "mystery" is not a secret to be hidden, but a profound truth that requires a ready heart to understand.

Bhagavad Gita 4.4.simpleEnglish: Arjuna asks Krishna a question: "You were born after the sun was born. So how can you have taught this knowledge first, before the sun existed?"
Bhagavad Gita 4.4.keyIdea: Arjuna is confused about how Krishna could have taught something ancient if Krishna was born later than the sun.
Bhagavad Gita 4.4.contextNote: This verse comes right after Krishna says he taught this knowledge long ago. Arjuna points out that Krishna appears to be a young man, born in recent times, so the claim seems impossible.

Bhagavad Gita 4.5.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that both of them have lived many lives before. Krishna remembers all of those past lives, but Arjuna does not.
Bhagavad Gita 4.5.keyIdea: Krishna claims to remember past births, while Arjuna does not.
Bhagavad Gita 4.5.contextNote: This verse introduces the idea that Krishna and Arjuna have existed in earlier forms. Krishna is saying he has knowledge that Arjuna lacks.

Bhagavad Gita 4.7.simpleEnglish: Whenever right action (dharma) grows weak and wrong action (adharma) grows strong, Krishna says he takes birth in the world to set things right.
Bhagavad Gita 4.7.keyIdea: Krishna describes why he appears in the world: to restore balance when wrongdoing overtakes rightdoing.
Bhagavad Gita 4.7.contextNote: This verse is Krishna's answer to why he is born again and again. It sets up the idea that divine action enters the world when human order breaks down.

Bhagavad Gita 4.8.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he is born again and again in each age. He comes to protect good people, to destroy those who do wrong, and to set up dharma (the right way to live).
Bhagavad Gita 4.8.keyIdea: Krishna describes why he takes birth repeatedly across time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.8.contextNote: This verse is Krishna's answer to Arjuna's question about Krishna's birth. Krishna is explaining his divine purpose for appearing in the world.

Bhagavad Gita 4.9.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna: whoever truly understands that Krishna's birth and actions are divine will cast off the body and not be born again. That person comes to Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 4.9.keyIdea: Understanding Krishna's divine nature leads to liberation from rebirth.
Bhagavad Gita 4.9.contextNote: This verse teaches that knowledge of Krishna's true nature—that his birth and deeds are divine, not ordinary—is the path to freedom from the cycle of rebirth. "Coming to Krishna" means reaching him or union with him.

Bhagavad Gita 4.10.simpleEnglish: Many people have let go of attachment, fear, and anger. They fill their minds with thoughts of Krishna (the speaker), depend on him, and have purified themselves through the discipline of knowledge. These people have come to share in his nature.
Bhagavad Gita 4.10.keyIdea: People who release attachment, fear, and anger, and who focus their minds on Krishna through knowledge and discipline, come to share in his essence.
Bhagavad Gita 4.10.contextNote: This verse describes a state of spiritual transformation—not a command, but a description of what happens when people practice detachment and knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 4.11.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: people come to me in different ways, and I meet them in those ways. However people approach me, I respond to them. In every way, people follow the path I show.
Bhagavad Gita 4.11.keyIdea: The divine responds to people according to how they seek it.
Bhagavad Gita 4.11.contextNote: This verse teaches that there is not one single way to approach the divine—different people may come with different devotion, understanding, or need, and the response meets them where they are.

Bhagavad Gita 4.12.simpleEnglish: People worship the gods because they want their work to succeed. In the human world, success from action comes quickly.
Bhagavad Gita 4.12.keyIdea: People often worship gods hoping for quick success in their work.
Bhagavad Gita 4.12.contextNote: This verse describes a common human practice—worshipping gods to gain success—without saying whether this is the best path or not.

Bhagavad Gita 4.13.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he created the four divisions of society (called varnas) based on people's qualities and the work they do. But even though he made this system, he says he is not bound by it—he stays free and unchanging.
Bhagavad Gita 4.13.keyIdea: The creator of a system is not trapped by it.
Bhagavad Gita 4.13.contextNote: This verse introduces the idea of varnas—a way of organizing society by type of work and qualities. Krishna claims to have set it up, but also claims to stand outside it. The tension between these two claims is part of what the Gita explores.

Bhagavad Gita 4.14.simpleEnglish: Krishna says that actions do not stain him, and he does not crave the results of actions. Whoever understands Krishna this way is not bound or trapped by their own actions.
Bhagavad Gita 4.14.keyIdea: Understanding that Krishna is not affected by actions or their results is the key to freedom from being trapped by one's own deeds.
Bhagavad Gita 4.14.contextNote: This verse teaches a principle about detachment from results. Krishna is explaining that he acts without being bound by consequences, and those who grasp this truth about him can also act without being enslaved by what happens.

Bhagavad Gita 4.15.simpleEnglish: People long ago who wanted to be free from the cycle of birth and death understood this truth and still did their work. So you should do your work too, just as those people did.
Bhagavad Gita 4.15.keyIdea: Even people seeking freedom from rebirth did their duty; you should do the same.
Bhagavad Gita 4.15.contextNote: This verse follows Krishna's teaching that action done without attachment to results is not binding. He now points to ancient examples to show this is not a new idea.

Bhagavad Gita 4.16.simpleEnglish: Even wise people get confused about what counts as action and what counts as inaction. So I will explain action to you. When you understand it, you will be free from harm.
Bhagavad Gita 4.16.keyIdea: Understanding the nature of action is the key to freedom.
Bhagavad Gita 4.16.contextNote: Krishna is saying that this is a deep question—not easy to answer. The verse promises that clarity about action will bring freedom, but does not yet explain what that clarity is.

Bhagavad Gita 4.17.simpleEnglish: You need to understand what action is. You need to understand what wrong action is. And you need to understand what inaction is. The truth about action is hard to see.
Bhagavad Gita 4.17.keyIdea: Understanding action—right action, wrong action, and inaction—is difficult and requires real knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 4.17.contextNote: Krishna is saying that action is not simple. It is not enough to just do things or not do things. You have to think carefully about what action really means.

Bhagavad Gita 4.18.simpleEnglish: A wise and devoted person can see something hidden in action and inaction. When you act, you can see inaction within it. When you do nothing, you can see action within it. This person performs all their duties with this understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 4.18.keyIdea: True wisdom is seeing the deeper nature of action and inaction at the same time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.18.contextNote: This verse describes a paradox: action contains inaction, and inaction contains action. The idea is that a wise person understands both the visible doing and something deeper beneath it.

Bhagavad Gita 4.19.simpleEnglish: The wise call someone learned when all their actions are free from desire and wishful thinking, and when knowledge burns away their deeds like fire.
Bhagavad Gita 4.19.keyIdea: True learning means acting without selfish desire, and letting knowledge consume your attachment to what you do.
Bhagavad Gita 4.19.contextNote: This verse describes what the wise recognize as real learning. The "fire of knowledge" is a metaphor for how understanding can burn away the ego's grip on our actions.

Bhagavad Gita 4.20.simpleEnglish: A person who lets go of wanting the results of their work, who feels satisfied no matter what, and who doesn't depend on others—that person does nothing wrong, even though they are busy working.
Bhagavad Gita 4.20.keyIdea: Acting without clinging to outcomes is a way to act without creating harm or debt.
Bhagavad Gita 4.20.contextNote: This verse describes a state of mind while working. The idea is that if you do your work but don't grip tightly to what you hope will happen, you stay free and clear.
difficultTerms: attachment to the fruit of action

Bhagavad Gita 4.21.simpleEnglish: A person who has no desires, who keeps their mind steady, and who gives up trying to own things does not gather sin when they work. They do only what the body needs to do.
Bhagavad Gita 4.21.keyIdea: Acting without greed or attachment does not create wrongdoing.
Bhagavad Gita 4.21.contextNote: This verse describes a way of living and working that Krishna teaches. The idea is that the *way* you act matters as much as *what* you do.

Bhagavad Gita 4.22.simpleEnglish: A person who is happy with whatever comes their way, who stays calm whether things go well or badly, and who does not feel jealous or angry—such a person is not trapped by their actions, even though they keep working.
Bhagavad Gita 4.22.keyIdea: Acting without being bound by results comes from accepting what life brings and staying balanced through both success and failure.
Bhagavad Gita 4.22.contextNote: This verse describes a state of mind that frees a person from being caught in the cycle of wanting and fearing outcomes. It is part of Krishna's teaching about how to act without attachment.

Bhagavad Gita 4.23.simpleEnglish: When someone acts without clinging to results, with a mind set on knowledge, and does their work as an offering (a sacrifice), all the karma from those actions dissolves away.
Bhagavad Gita 4.23.keyIdea: Actions done without attachment and with the right intention do not bind a person to karma.
Bhagavad Gita 4.23.contextNote: The verse teaches that the way you act matters as much as what you do. If you act freely, with understanding, and in service rather than for personal gain, the usual consequences of action do not stick to you.

Bhagavad Gita 4.25.simpleEnglish: Different people make offerings in different ways. Some offer to the gods. Others offer the sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman (the ultimate reality)—using sacrifice as the sacrifice.
Bhagavad Gita 4.25.keyIdea: There are different paths of devotion, and the verse describes two of them.
Bhagavad Gita 4.25.contextNote: This verse is part of a longer teaching about sacrifice. It shows that Krishna is describing varieties of spiritual practice, not ranking them.

Bhagavad Gita 4.24.simpleEnglish: In a sacrifice, every part is Brahman (the ultimate reality). The offering is Brahman. The tool used to offer it is Brahman. The fire is Brahman. The person making the offering is Brahman. When someone acts with this understanding—seeing Brahman in everything they do—they reach Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 4.24.keyIdea: When you see the ultimate reality in every part of an action, the action itself becomes a path to that reality.
Bhagavad Gita 4.24.contextNote: This verse uses the language of sacrifice as a way to teach about awareness. It does not require literal sacrifice; it describes a state of mind in which someone recognizes the sacred in all their actions.

Bhagavad Gita 4.26.simpleEnglish: Some people practice by controlling their senses—like hearing and the others—and offer them up like a sacrifice in the fire of self-restraint. Other people offer up the things their senses enjoy—like sounds and other objects—into the fire of their senses themselves.
Bhagavad Gita 4.26.keyIdea: Different paths of spiritual practice use the senses and self-control in different ways.
Bhagavad Gita 4.26.contextNote: This verse describes two approaches to spiritual discipline. The first controls the senses themselves; the second lets the senses experience their objects but burns away attachment to them. Both are forms of sacrifice (yajna).

Bhagavad Gita 4.27.simpleEnglish: Some people offer up all the work of their senses and their breath into a fire of devotion. They do this through self-restraint, and knowledge lights that fire. It is like they are giving everything they do and everything they are to something higher.
Bhagavad Gita 4.27.keyIdea: A person can dedicate all their actions and their very life to a spiritual goal through discipline and understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 4.27.contextNote: The verse uses the image of a fire sacrifice (a ritual offering). Here, instead of burning things in a physical fire, a person "burns" their own actions and life-force as an offering through discipline and wisdom.

Bhagavad Gita 4.28.simpleEnglish: Some people offer wealth as a sacrifice. Others practice hard discipline, or concentrate their mind, or study the Vedas (ancient texts), or pursue knowledge. Some are ascetics (people who live simply and follow strict rules) devoted to their practice.
Bhagavad Gita 4.28.keyIdea: Different people practice different kinds of sacrifice and discipline.
Bhagavad Gita 4.28.contextNote: This verse lists various ways people can dedicate themselves spiritually—through giving, discipline, meditation, study, and strict living.

Bhagavad Gita 4.31.simpleEnglish: People who make offerings and sacrifices (yajña) reach the eternal world. But this world—the one we live in now—is not even for those who do not sacrifice. So how could they reach any other world?
Bhagavad Gita 4.31.keyIdea: Without sacrifice or offering, a person cannot prosper even in this life, let alone in any world beyond.
Bhagavad Gita 4.31.contextNote: Krishna is saying that sacrifice (yajña) is necessary for a good life. The word "sacrifice" here means ritual offering and action done with devotion, not just religious ceremony.

Bhagavad Gita 4.29.simpleEnglish: Some yogis offer one breath-force into another—the upward breath into the downward, or the downward into the upward. Others control both breath-forces by stopping their motion and focus on breath-practice. Still others eat only what they need and offer their life-breath into itself. All these people know sacrifice, and sacrifice burns away their faults.
Bhagavad Gita 4.29.keyIdea: Different yogis practice different forms of breath-control and self-discipline as a kind of sacrifice.
Bhagavad Gita 4.29.contextNote: The verse describes yogic practices (prāṇāyāma) as forms of sacrifice. "Upward" and "downward" life-breaths refer to vital energies in the body that yogis work with. The idea is that disciplined practice itself can purify a person.

Bhagavad Gita 4.32.simpleEnglish: The Vedas (ancient Hindu texts) describe many different kinds of sacrifice. All of them come from action—from doing things. When you understand this, you become free.
Bhagavad Gita 4.32.keyIdea: Understanding that all sacrifices arise from action leads to freedom.
Bhagavad Gita 4.32.contextNote: Krishna is explaining that sacrifice is not a single rigid practice, but many forms rooted in human action. Knowing this truth brings liberation.

Bhagavad Gita 4.30.simpleEnglish: Some people offer their breath into their breath as a sacrifice. Others offer their senses or their life-force into the senses. All of these people know about sacrifice, and the sacrifice destroys their sins. Those who eat what is left over from the sacrifice reach the eternal Brahman (the ultimate reality).
Bhagavad Gita 4.30.keyIdea: Different kinds of sacrifice—whether physical or inner—can purify a person and lead toward the eternal.
Bhagavad Gita 4.30.contextNote: This verse describes several forms of sacrifice. The first part names practices like controlling the breath or offering the senses. The second part says that all who practice sacrifice with knowledge are purified by it, and those who consume the sacred leftovers reach Brahman.

Bhagavad Gita 4.33.simpleEnglish: A sacrifice of knowledge is better than a sacrifice of wealth, Krishna tells Arjuna. All action, he says, is fully understood through knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 4.33.keyIdea: Understanding through knowledge is more valuable than giving material things.
Bhagavad Gita 4.33.contextNote: In the Gita, "sacrifice" (yajña) means an offering or practice done with focus. Krishna is comparing two kinds: giving wealth versus gaining understanding. He says understanding matters more because it shows you what all actions really are.

Bhagavad Gita 4.34.simpleEnglish: To learn real knowledge, you need to approach wise people with respect, ask them honest questions, and serve them. People who truly understand the truth will teach you.
Bhagavad Gita 4.34.keyIdea: Wisdom comes through respect, curiosity, and service to those who understand.
Bhagavad Gita 4.34.contextNote: This verse describes how a student should learn from a teacher—not by demanding answers, but through respectful engagement.

Bhagavad Gita 4.36.simpleEnglish: Even if you have done more wrong than anyone else, knowledge can carry you across it all—like a boat crossing water.
Bhagavad Gita 4.36.keyIdea: Knowledge is described as a way to move past wrongdoing, no matter how much.
Bhagavad Gita 4.36.contextNote: The verse uses the image of a boat to show how knowledge works. It does not say wrongdoing disappears, but that knowledge helps you cross over it.

Bhagavad Gita 4.38.simpleEnglish: Nothing in the world purifies a person like knowledge does. When someone practices devotion steadily, they find this knowledge within themselves over time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.38.keyIdea: Knowledge is the most powerful way to purify the mind, and it comes through devoted practice.
Bhagavad Gita 4.38.contextNote: The verse speaks of knowledge (jñāna) as a spiritual tool—not just learning facts, but understanding that transforms a person from within.

Bhagavad Gita 4.35.simpleEnglish: Once you understand this knowledge, you will not fall into confusion again, Arjuna (a warrior in the Mahabharata). Through it, you will see all living beings first within yourself, and then in me (Krishna, the speaker).
Bhagavad Gita 4.35.keyIdea: Understanding this teaching brings clarity and a way of seeing all beings as connected.
Bhagavad Gita 4.35.contextNote: This verse promises that the knowledge Krishna has been teaching will free Arjuna from delusion and give him a new way of perceiving all living things.

Bhagavad Gita 4.37.simpleEnglish: A bright fire turns wood into ash. In the same way, the fire of knowledge turns all actions into ash. This means that true understanding can free a person from the results of past deeds.
Bhagavad Gita 4.37.keyIdea: Knowledge destroys the binding power of actions, just as fire destroys fuel.
Bhagavad Gita 4.37.contextNote: The verse uses a comparison (fire and ash) to explain how wisdom works. It does not mean actions literally disappear, but that understanding changes how they affect a person's future.

Bhagavad Gita 4.39.simpleEnglish: A person who has faith, controls their senses, and works hard can gain knowledge. Once they have that knowledge, they reach the highest peace quickly.
Bhagavad Gita 4.39.keyIdea: Faith, discipline, and effort lead to knowledge, which brings deep peace.
Bhagavad Gita 4.39.contextNote: This verse describes a path: first faith and self-control, then knowledge, then peace. It is not saying these things happen by accident.

Bhagavad Gita 4.40.simpleEnglish: A person who does not know, does not have faith, and is full of doubt will be ruined. Someone whose self is full of doubt cannot find happiness in this world, the next world, or anywhere.
Bhagavad Gita 4.40.keyIdea: Doubt and lack of faith destroy a person's chance for happiness.
Bhagavad Gita 4.40.contextNote: Krishna is explaining what happens to someone who refuses to learn and trust. The verse uses "ruined" and "next world" (the afterlife in Hindu belief) to show the seriousness of the problem.

Bhagavad Gita 5.2.simpleEnglish: Krishna says that both renunciation (giving up action) and karma yoga (disciplined action) lead to happiness. But karma yoga is better than renunciation.
Bhagavad Gita 5.2.keyIdea: Both paths can work, but engaged action is superior to withdrawal.
Bhagavad Gita 5.2.contextNote: This verse answers a question about whether it is better to stop acting or to act with discipline. Krishna is comparing two spiritual approaches.

Bhagavad Gita 4.41.simpleEnglish: A person who has given their actions to devotion, destroyed doubt through knowledge, and is self-possessed—actions do not bind or trap that person. They are free.
Bhagavad Gita 4.41.keyIdea: When someone acts without ego and has cleared away doubt, their actions don't create a hold over them.
Bhagavad Gita 4.41.contextNote: The verse teaches that actions only bind us when we act from ego and confusion. A person who acts with devotion and clear knowledge remains free.

Bhagavad Gita 5.1.simpleEnglish: Arjuna asks Krishna a question. Krishna, you say that giving up actions is good. But you also say that doing actions is good. Which one is actually better? Please tell me clearly.
Bhagavad Gita 5.1.keyIdea: Arjuna is confused because Krishna seems to praise two opposite paths.
Bhagavad Gita 5.1.contextNote: This is the start of Chapter 5. Arjuna wants a straight answer about whether it is better to stop doing things or to keep doing them.

Bhagavad Gita 4.42.simpleEnglish: Doubt and confusion come from not knowing the truth. Knowledge is like a sword that can cut through them. So use what you understand to clear away your doubts, and then act with full commitment.
Bhagavad Gita 4.42.keyIdea: Knowledge destroys doubt; then you can act with confidence.
Bhagavad Gita 4.42.contextNote: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, who is paralyzed by doubt about whether he should fight. The verse says that understanding the truth is the tool to cut through confusion.

Bhagavad Gita 5.3.simpleEnglish: A person who has no hatred and no craving is truly an ascetic (someone who has given up worldly desires), even if they live in the world. When you stop pulling in opposite directions—wanting some things and rejecting others—you become free from the bonds that tie you down.
Bhagavad Gita 5.3.keyIdea: True renunciation is not about leaving home; it is about letting go of likes and dislikes.
Bhagavad Gita 5.3.contextNote: Krishna is explaining that the real mark of an ascetic is inner freedom from craving and aversion, not outer appearance or lifestyle.

Bhagavad Gita 5.4.simpleEnglish: Only children say that sankhya (the path of knowledge) and yoga (the path of practice) are completely different. A wise person knows that if you follow either one well, you get the good results of both.
Bhagavad Gita 5.4.keyIdea: The two paths lead to the same goal when practiced sincerely.
Bhagavad Gita 5.4.contextNote: Krishna is saying that sankhya and yoga are not opposites—they work together. Doing one properly includes the benefits of the other.

Bhagavad Gita 5.6.simpleEnglish: Renunciation (giving up worldly life) is hard to achieve without devotion. But a wise person who practices devotion reaches Brahman (the ultimate reality) quickly.
Bhagavad Gita 5.6.keyIdea: Devotion makes the spiritual path easier and faster than trying to renounce the world without it.
Bhagavad Gita 5.6.contextNote: Krishna is telling Arjuna that simply walking away from life does not work. The inner practice of devotion is what actually leads to spiritual realization.

Bhagavad Gita 5.5.simpleEnglish: The goal that people reach through one path (called sankhya, or knowledge) can also be reached through another path (called yoga, or practice). Someone who understands that both paths lead to the same place—that they are really one thing—sees the truth.
Bhagavad Gita 5.5.keyIdea: Two different spiritual paths can lead to the same destination.
Bhagavad Gita 5.5.contextNote: Sankhya and yoga are two ways of spiritual practice taught in Indian philosophy. This verse says they are not opposites, but two ways up the same mountain.

Bhagavad Gita 5.7.simpleEnglish: A person who practices yoga (discipline and focus), has a pure heart, controls their own mind and senses, and sees themselves in all living beings—this person does not become stained by their actions, even while acting in the world.
Bhagavad Gita 5.7.keyIdea: Actions do not bind or corrupt a person who acts with a pure heart and sees the same self in all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 5.7.contextNote: This verse describes a state of inner freedom. The idea is that someone who has trained their mind and heart deeply does not become trapped or harmed by the work they do.

Bhagavad Gita 5.8.simpleEnglish: A person who understands the truth and is devoted to yoga thinks: "I am not doing anything." This is what they think even while they see, hear, touch, smell, eat, move, sleep, and breathe.
Bhagavad Gita 5.8.keyIdea: A wise person recognizes that the body and senses act on their own, separate from the true self.
Bhagavad Gita 5.8.contextNote: This verse introduces a key teaching: the person who knows the difference between the unchanging self and the changing body can watch all physical actions happen without claiming "I am the doer." The verse continues in the next line with more examples of action.

Bhagavad Gita 5.9.simpleEnglish: A person talks, throws things, picks things up, opens and closes their eyes. But they understand that the senses are just doing their job—touching, seeing, hearing, tasting, and smelling things around them.
Bhagavad Gita 5.9.keyIdea: The senses naturally interact with the world; a wise person sees this clearly without being confused by it.
Bhagavad Gita 5.9.contextNote: This verse describes how someone can act and perceive in the world while keeping a clear mind about what is actually happening.

Bhagavad Gita 5.10.simpleEnglish: When someone does their work but does not hold tight to the results, and gives the work to Brahman (the ultimate reality), sin does not stick to them. It is like water rolling off a lotus leaf without making it wet.
Bhagavad Gita 5.10.keyIdea: Doing work without attachment and with dedication to something larger protects a person from being harmed by wrongdoing.
Bhagavad Gita 5.10.contextNote: The verse uses the lotus leaf as a picture of how detachment works—the leaf stays clean because water cannot cling to it. Here, sin is like the water.

Bhagavad Gita 5.12.simpleEnglish: A person who is devoted and lets go of wanting the results of their actions finds deep peace. A person who is not devoted and stays attached to the results gets trapped by their own desires.
Bhagavad Gita 5.12.keyIdea: Letting go of wanting results from your actions brings peace; holding on to those desires keeps you trapped.
Bhagavad Gita 5.12.contextNote: This verse contrasts two ways of acting: one where you do what you do without clinging to what comes from it, and one where you act mainly to get what you want.

Bhagavad Gita 5.11.simpleEnglish: People who practice yoga do their work with their body, mind, and senses. But they let go of attachment to the results. They do this to make their inner self pure and clear.
Bhagavad Gita 5.11.keyIdea: Doing work without clinging to what it brings you can purify the inner self.
Bhagavad Gita 5.11.contextNote: The verse describes a way of acting: you work fully, but you don't hold tight to wanting a reward or fearing a loss. This detachment is said to clean the spirit.

Bhagavad Gita 5.13.simpleEnglish: A person who controls their mind can live at peace in the body—which is like a city with nine gates (the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, and two lower openings). By letting go of the need to act, they neither do things nor make others do them.
Bhagavad Gita 5.13.keyIdea: Inner peace comes from controlling the mind and releasing the urge to act.
Bhagavad Gita 5.13.contextNote: This verse uses the body as a metaphor for a city. The "nine portals" are the body's openings through which the senses connect to the world. "Renouncing all actions by the mind" means releasing the mental drive to control or change things.

Bhagavad Gita 5.14.simpleEnglish: The Lord does not make people act, and does not make actions happen. The Lord does not tie actions to their results. Nature itself keeps working and moving.
Bhagavad Gita 5.14.keyIdea: God does not control actions or their outcomes; nature operates on its own.
Bhagavad Gita 5.14.contextNote: This verse appears in a section where Krishna explains that the wise see beyond the surface of action. The point is that the divine does not micromanage the world—natural law does.

Bhagavad Gita 5.16.simpleEnglish: When someone destroys their ignorance through knowledge of the self, that knowledge shines like the sun. It lights up the supreme principle for them.
Bhagavad Gita 5.16.keyIdea: Knowledge of the self is like sunlight that reveals what is highest and most real.
Bhagavad Gita 5.16.contextNote: The verse compares the power of self-knowledge to the sun's brightness. Just as the sun reveals what is hidden in darkness, knowledge of the self reveals the supreme principle.

Bhagavad Gita 5.15.simpleEnglish: The Lord does not take on anyone's sin or good deeds. Knowledge gets covered up by ignorance, and that is why all living beings become confused.
Bhagavad Gita 5.15.keyIdea: Ignorance, not the Lord, is what clouds people's understanding.
Bhagavad Gita 5.15.contextNote: This verse teaches that the Lord is not responsible for people's actions or their confusion. Instead, ignorance itself is what hides knowledge and leads beings astray.

Bhagavad Gita 5.17.simpleEnglish: People whose mind, self, and whole life are centred on the divine (what Krishna calls "it") reach a state where they do not return to the cycle of birth and death. Knowledge destroys their sins and faults.
Bhagavad Gita 5.17.keyIdea: Complete devotion to the divine, guided by knowledge, leads to liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
Bhagavad Gita 5.17.contextNote: This verse describes the result of the spiritual path Krishna has been teaching. "It" refers to the divine reality discussed in the verses before this one.

Bhagavad Gita 5.18.simpleEnglish: A wise person sees all beings the same way. A learned and humble Brahmin (a member of the priestly class), a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person of the lowest caste—the wise person looks at them all with equal respect.
Bhagavad Gita 5.18.keyIdea: The wise see the same worth in all living beings, no matter their status or kind.
Bhagavad Gita 5.18.contextNote: This verse teaches that true wisdom means not judging beings by their rank, wealth, or caste. It challenges the social order of ancient India by saying that a wise person does not rank one being above another.

Bhagavad Gita 5.20.simpleEnglish: A person who understands Brahman (the ultimate reality) and stays calm and clear-minded does not get excited when something good happens, and does not get upset when something bad happens. Their mind stays steady either way.
Bhagavad Gita 5.20.keyIdea: A steady mind rooted in understanding Brahman remains balanced through both pleasant and unpleasant experiences.
Bhagavad Gita 5.20.contextNote: The verse describes a quality of mind—not indifference or numbness, but a kind of stability that comes from a deeper understanding of reality.

Bhagavad Gita 5.19.simpleEnglish: People who keep their mind calm and balanced have already won over the world around them, even while living in it. Brahman (the ultimate reality) is perfect and the same everywhere. So those who stay balanced are resting in Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 5.19.keyIdea: A balanced mind is a kind of victory, because it connects you to what is perfect and unchanging.
Bhagavad Gita 5.19.contextNote: This verse teaches that inner balance is not something you achieve after leaving the world—it is a way of being in the world right now.

Bhagavad Gita 5.21.simpleEnglish: A person whose mind is not caught up in wanting things from outside finds happiness inside themselves. When that person's mind joins with Brahman (the ultimate reality) through steady focus, they find a happiness that never runs out.
Bhagavad Gita 5.21.keyIdea: Inner happiness that comes from not chasing external things is deeper and lasting than happiness that depends on the outside world.
Bhagavad Gita 5.21.contextNote: This verse contrasts two kinds of happiness: one that depends on things outside us, and one that comes from within and stays steady.

Bhagavad Gita 5.22.simpleEnglish: When your senses touch something—like tasting food or seeing something beautiful—you feel pleasure. But these pleasures come and go, and they often bring pain too. A wise person knows this, so they don't get caught up chasing them.
Bhagavad Gita 5.22.keyIdea: Pleasures from the senses are temporary and mixed with suffering.
Bhagavad Gita 5.22.contextNote: The verse is part of Krishna's teaching about what brings real happiness. He is saying that ordinary pleasures—the kind everyone chases—are not reliable or deep.

Bhagavad Gita 5.23.simpleEnglish: A person who can stay calm when desire and anger push at them—even while still alive in their body—is devoted and happy. This is not about never feeling these things. It is about not letting them control what you do.
Bhagavad Gita 5.23.keyIdea: Mastering your reactions to desire and anger, while you are still living, is a sign of devotion and real happiness.
Bhagavad Gita 5.23.contextNote: The verse speaks of "before release from the body"—meaning while you are still alive. It teaches that the work of self-control happens now, in this life, not after death.

Bhagavad Gita 5.24.simpleEnglish: A person who finds happiness inside themselves, finds rest inside themselves, and finds their own light of knowledge inside themselves—this person becomes one with Brahman (the ultimate reality) and reaches the peace that comes from that unity.
Bhagavad Gita 5.24.keyIdea: True peace comes from finding completeness within yourself, not from outside things.
Bhagavad Gita 5.24.contextNote: This verse describes a state of inner self-sufficiency. The person does not need external sources for happiness, rest, or understanding. This inner completeness is what allows them to realize their connection to Brahman.

Bhagavad Gita 5.26.simpleEnglish: People who have given up wanting things and getting angry, who control their minds, and who understand their own self—they find peace that comes from Brahman (the ultimate reality). This peace is with them whether they are alive or after they die.
Bhagavad Gita 5.26.keyIdea: Inner peace comes to those who let go of desire and anger and know themselves.
Bhagavad Gita 5.26.contextNote: The verse describes a state of freedom that does not depend on what happens to the body. The "both sides" means in life and after death.

Bhagavad Gita 5.25.simpleEnglish: Sages (wise people) who have let go of their wrongdoing, who have stopped doubting themselves, who control their own minds, and who care about the welfare of all living beings—these people reach a state of deep peace called Brahmic bliss.
Bhagavad Gita 5.25.keyIdea: People who purify themselves inwardly and work for the good of all beings attain a profound spiritual peace.
Bhagavad Gita 5.25.contextNote: This verse describes the result of the spiritual path described earlier in chapter 5. It shows what happens when someone combines inner discipline with compassion for all living things.

Bhagavad Gita 5.28.simpleEnglish: A person who controls their senses, mind, and understanding, and whose only goal is freedom from the cycle of birth and death, has no desire, fear, or anger. Such a person is always free.
Bhagavad Gita 5.28.keyIdea: Freedom comes from controlling the senses and mind, and letting go of desire, fear, and anger.
Bhagavad Gita 5.28.contextNote: The verse describes a state of inner freedom that is not about running away from life, but about mastering one's own reactions and attachments.

Bhagavad Gita 5.27.simpleEnglish: A wise person turns away from things outside the body. They focus their eyes between the eyebrows. They make the breath that goes up and the breath that goes down move at the same speed, keeping both breaths moving only through the nose.
Bhagavad Gita 5.27.keyIdea: This describes a meditation practice where the mind and senses are controlled and turned inward.
Bhagavad Gita 5.27.contextNote: This verse is part of a teaching about how a person can reach freedom through discipline of the mind and senses. The practices named here—focusing the gaze, balancing the breath—are techniques meant to steady the mind.

Bhagavad Gita 5.29.simpleEnglish: When someone understands that Krishna is the one who receives all sacrifices and penances, the great ruler of all worlds, and a friend to all living beings, that person finds peace.
Bhagavad Gita 5.29.keyIdea: Understanding Krishna as the receiver of all offerings and friend to all beings leads to inner peace.
Bhagavad Gita 5.29.contextNote: This verse describes a spiritual understanding—that recognizing Krishna's role in all worship and his care for all creatures brings calm to the mind.

Bhagavad Gita 6.1.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: A person who does the work they should do, without worrying about whether it will bring them reward or harm, is truly a renouncer and a yogi (someone on a spiritual path). It is not someone who simply stops making fires or stops working altogether.
Bhagavad Gita 6.1.keyIdea: True renunciation means doing your duty without attachment to results, not abandoning action.
Bhagavad Gita 6.1.contextNote: This verse introduces a key teaching: giving up the desire for rewards is different from giving up work itself. The "sacred fires" refer to ritual duties.

Bhagavad Gita 6.3.simpleEnglish: A person who wants to reach yoga (a state of inner focus and connection) should use action—doing their duties—as the path. Once they have reached that state, tranquility becomes their path instead.
Bhagavad Gita 6.3.keyIdea: The way forward changes depending on where you are on the path.
Bhagavad Gita 6.3.contextNote: Yoga here means a spiritual state, not physical postures. The verse suggests that beginners need to act and engage, while those further along need to cultivate inner peace.

Bhagavad Gita 6.2.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (the son of Pandu) that what people call renunciation—giving things up—is really the same as devotion. No one can truly be devoted if they still hold on to all their desires and plans.
Bhagavad Gita 6.2.keyIdea: Renunciation and devotion are not separate; devotion requires letting go of personal desires.
Bhagavad Gita 6.2.contextNote: This verse opens a discussion about yoga (spiritual practice). Krishna is saying that the inner work of yoga—giving up attachment to your own wants—is what renunciation truly means.

Bhagavad Gita 6.5.simpleEnglish: A person should lift themselves up through their own effort. They should not drag themselves down. Your own self can be your best friend, or it can be your worst enemy.
Bhagavad Gita 6.5.keyIdea: You have the power to help yourself or harm yourself through your own choices.
Bhagavad Gita 6.5.contextNote: This verse is about self-discipline and the power of your own mind and will. It does not say how to lift yourself up—that comes in the verses that follow.

Bhagavad Gita 6.4.simpleEnglish: When someone stops chasing after things the senses want—tastes, sights, sounds, and so on—and stops clinging to the results of their actions, they have reached a state called yoga (a joining or steadiness of mind). This happens when they let go of all their desires and plans.
Bhagavad Gita 6.4.keyIdea: Yoga is a state of mind reached by releasing attachment to sense-pleasures and the fruits of action.
Bhagavad Gita 6.4.contextNote: The verse describes what it means to be "established in yoga"—not a physical practice, but a mental condition of non-attachment.

Bhagavad Gita 6.6.simpleEnglish: When you control your own mind and desires, your self becomes your friend. But when you do not control yourself, your own self acts like an enemy against you.
Bhagavad Gita 6.6.keyIdea: Your self can be either your greatest friend or your worst enemy, depending on whether you master it or let it master you.
Bhagavad Gita 6.6.contextNote: This verse uses "self" to mean your inner nature—your thoughts, impulses, and desires. It is not about being selfish or self-centered, but about the struggle between discipline and lack of control within one person.

Bhagavad Gita 6.7.simpleEnglish: A person who has brought their own mind under control and become calm can keep their attention steady. This stays true even when they face cold or heat, pleasure or pain, respect or disrespect.
Bhagavad Gita 6.7.keyIdea: Self-control and inner calm let a person stay focused no matter what happens around them.
Bhagavad Gita 6.7.contextNote: This verse describes a quality of someone who has trained their mind. It is part of Krishna's teaching on yoga (a path of practice and discipline).

Bhagavad Gita 6.9.simpleEnglish: A person is considered highest when they see all people the same way—whether those people are friends, enemies, strangers, or relatives. They treat the good and the bad with the same even mind.
Bhagavad Gita 6.9.keyIdea: True excellence comes from treating all people equally, without favoring some over others.
Bhagavad Gita 6.9.contextNote: This verse describes a quality of a yogi (a person practicing yoga, or spiritual discipline). It does not mean being cold or uncaring, but rather not letting personal likes and dislikes cloud your judgment or actions.

Bhagavad Gita 6.8.simpleEnglish: A yogi (someone who practices yoga) is someone whose mind is satisfied by knowledge and understanding, who stays calm and steady, who controls their senses, and who sees a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equally worthless. These are the marks of a person truly devoted to yoga.
Bhagavad Gita 6.8.keyIdea: True yoga means having a mind at peace with knowledge, steady emotions, controlled senses, and no attachment to wealth or status.
Bhagavad Gita 6.8.contextNote: The verse lists qualities that show when someone has reached a real state of yoga—not just physical postures, but inner balance and freedom from craving.

Bhagavad Gita 6.11.simpleEnglish: A person who wants to meditate should find a clean place and set up a firm seat there. The seat should not be too high or too low. It should be covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass (a sacred grass used in rituals).
Bhagavad Gita 6.11.keyIdea: The verse describes the physical setup needed for meditation practice.
Bhagavad Gita 6.11.contextNote: This is part of Krishna's teaching on yoga (meditation and spiritual practice). The details about the seat show that the practice requires care and preparation.

Bhagavad Gita 6.10.simpleEnglish: A person who practices yoga should work on their mind and self all the time. They do this alone, in a quiet place, keeping their thoughts steady. They should not expect rewards and should not hold on to things they own.
Bhagavad Gita 6.10.keyIdea: Yoga practice requires solitude, mental discipline, freedom from desire, and non-attachment to possessions.
Bhagavad Gita 6.10.contextNote: This verse describes the outer conditions and inner attitudes that support yoga practice. It is not saying a yogi must never leave their room, but that focused practice needs quiet and freedom from distraction.

Bhagavad Gita 6.12.simpleEnglish: Sit on a seat and focus your mind on one thing only. Keep your thoughts and senses under control. Practice this way to purify yourself.
Bhagavad Gita 6.12.keyIdea: Focused practice with a calm mind and controlled senses leads to inner purity.
Bhagavad Gita 6.12.contextNote: This verse describes the physical and mental setup for yoga practice. "Purity of self" means clarity and freedom from distraction.

Bhagavad Gita 6.13.simpleEnglish: Keep your body, head, and neck straight and still. Look at the tip of your own nose. Do not let your eyes wander to other places.
Bhagavad Gita 6.13.keyIdea: This describes how to sit when you are practicing meditation or yoga.
Bhagavad Gita 6.13.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching on yoga practice. It gives practical instructions for the body position and where to direct your gaze.

Bhagavad Gita 6.16.simpleEnglish: Yoga (a practice of discipline and focus) does not work for someone who eats too much or too little. It also does not work for someone who sleeps too much or stays awake all the time. Balance matters.
Bhagavad Gita 6.16.keyIdea: Yoga requires balance in eating and sleeping, not extremes.
Bhagavad Gita 6.16.contextNote: Krishna is teaching Arjuna about the conditions needed for yoga to succeed. This verse warns against going to extremes in daily habits.

Bhagavad Gita 6.15.simpleEnglish: A person who keeps practicing yoga (meditation and discipline) with a steady, controlled mind finds deep peace. This peace leads to freedom from suffering and unity with Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 6.15.keyIdea: Regular practice of yoga with a focused mind brings lasting peace and spiritual freedom.
Bhagavad Gita 6.15.contextNote: The verse describes what happens when someone practices yoga consistently—their mind becomes calm, and they experience a state of peace that the text calls "final emancipation" (freedom from the cycle of suffering).

Bhagavad Gita 6.14.simpleEnglish: A person who wants to join with the divine should be calm inside and free from fear. They should follow the rules of a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacharya). They should control their mind and focus it on Krishna. Then they should sit in practice, treating Krishna as their highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 6.14.keyIdea: The verse describes how someone should prepare their mind and body to reach the divine through discipline and focus.
Bhagavad Gita 6.14.contextNote: This verse is Krishna's instruction on the method of yoga—not just physical postures, but a way of training the mind and senses. "Brahmacharya" refers to a student's life of discipline and celibacy, but here it means following rules of restraint and purity.

Bhagavad Gita 6.17.simpleEnglish: Yoga—the practice of steadying the mind—destroys suffering when a person eats the right amount, moves their body in the right way, works carefully, and sleeps and wakes at the right times. Balance in these everyday things is the path.
Bhagavad Gita 6.17.keyIdea: Yoga works when life is balanced: food, movement, work, and rest all in their proper measure.
Bhagavad Gita 6.17.contextNote: This verse teaches that yoga is not only meditation or posture. It includes how you live day to day—eating, exercising, working, and sleeping in a measured, thoughtful way.

Bhagavad Gita 6.18.simpleEnglish: When someone's mind is calm and stays focused on their own self, and they stop wanting things from the world around them, that person is called devoted or steady in their practice.
Bhagavad Gita 6.18.keyIdea: A steady mind that stops chasing desires is the mark of real devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 6.18.contextNote: This verse describes what it means to be "devoted" (yukta) in the practice of yoga—not as belief or worship, but as a state of mind that is calm, focused, and free from craving.

Bhagavad Gita 6.19.simpleEnglish: A lamp in a still room does not flicker. This is like a person who practices yoga (a discipline of mind and body) and keeps their mind steady and calm. Their mind stays focused, like the lamp stays still.
Bhagavad Gita 6.19.keyIdea: A steady mind in yoga practice is compared to a lamp that does not flicker in still air.
Bhagavad Gita 6.19.contextNote: The verse uses the image of a lamp to explain what a calm, focused mind looks like during spiritual practice.

Bhagavad Gita 6.21.simpleEnglish: There is a happiness so deep that the senses cannot touch it—only the mind can know it. When someone finds this, they do not waver from the truth. They think nothing else matters more.
Bhagavad Gita 6.21.keyIdea: The deepest happiness comes from understanding, not from what the senses feel.
Bhagavad Gita 6.21.contextNote: This verse describes a state of inner peace that goes beyond physical pleasure. It is found through the mind and understanding, not through the body.

Bhagavad Gita 6.20.simpleEnglish: When you practice yoga and meditation, your mind becomes still and stops its usual chatter. In that quiet state, you can see your own self clearly, and you feel content just being yourself.
Bhagavad Gita 6.20.keyIdea: Deep meditation brings a calm mind and a sense of peace with who you are.
Bhagavad Gita 6.20.contextNote: This verse describes a state of mind that comes from yoga practice—not a goal you must reach, but a condition that can happen when the mind settles.

Bhagavad Gita 6.22.simpleEnglish: When you find this state of mind, you think there is nothing better. Once you are steady in it, even great suffering cannot shake you. This is what yoga (a joining or union of the mind with the divine) really means—a state where pain no longer has power over you.
Bhagavad Gita 6.22.keyIdea: True yoga is a state of mind so stable that even serious suffering cannot disturb it.
Bhagavad Gita 6.22.contextNote: This verse describes the goal of the yoga practice Krishna has been teaching. It is not about physical postures, but about training the mind to stay calm and centered.

Bhagavad Gita 6.23.simpleEnglish: Yoga (the practice of steadying the mind) means breaking free from suffering. You should practice it with firm resolve and without losing hope.
Bhagavad Gita 6.23.keyIdea: Yoga is the discipline of separating yourself from suffering through steady, determined practice.
Bhagavad Gita 6.23.contextNote: The verse defines what yoga really is—not just postures, but a way to move away from pain. It then says how to do it: with commitment and without giving up.

Bhagavad Gita 6.24.simpleEnglish: Let go of all desires that come from imagination and wishes. Use your mind to hold back all your senses from every direction.
Bhagavad Gita 6.24.keyIdea: The practice described here is to release desires born from mental fancies and to control the senses through the mind.
Bhagavad Gita 6.24.contextNote: This verse describes a step in the yoga practice Krishna is teaching—not rejecting the senses themselves, but training the mind to govern them.

Bhagavad Gita 6.25.simpleEnglish: Step by step, with a steady mind and courage, you become calm. You fix your mind on your own self. Then you think of nothing else.
Bhagavad Gita 6.25.keyIdea: Quieting the mind takes patience, firmness, and turning your attention inward.
Bhagavad Gita 6.25.contextNote: This verse describes a practice of meditation: gradual, deliberate, with mental discipline. It is part of Krishna's teaching on yoga (the practice of training the mind and body).

Bhagavad Gita 6.26.simpleEnglish: The mind jumps around and wanders. Whenever you notice it running off, bring it back. Keep bringing it back to yourself, again and again, until it stays steady.
Bhagavad Gita 6.26.keyIdea: Training the mind means catching it when it wanders and gently returning it to focus.
Bhagavad Gita 6.26.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching on meditation and mental discipline. "The self" here means your own inner awareness or presence.

Bhagavad Gita 6.27.simpleEnglish: A person who practices yoga and has a calm, peaceful mind reaches the highest happiness. This happens when the restless, passionate part of their nature has been quieted, and they are free from wrongdoing. In this state, they become united with Brahman (the ultimate reality).
Bhagavad Gita 6.27.keyIdea: Deep peace and unity with ultimate reality come to those whose minds are calm and whose passions are controlled.
Bhagavad Gita 6.27.contextNote: This verse describes the result of the yoga practice discussed in chapter 6. It shows what happens when a person successfully stills their mind and overcomes restless desires.

Bhagavad Gita 6.28.simpleEnglish: A person who keeps practicing yoga (joining the mind to the divine) stays free from wrongdoing. Through this practice, they reach a deep happiness—a direct touch with Brahman (the ultimate reality).
Bhagavad Gita 6.28.keyIdea: Steady practice of yoga leads to freedom from sin and the highest happiness.
Bhagavad Gita 6.28.contextNote: This verse describes the result of the yoga practice Krishna has been teaching. "Contact with Brahman" means a direct experience of the divine reality.

Bhagavad Gita 6.29.simpleEnglish: A person who practices yoga and meditation sees the same self in all living things, and sees all living things in that one self. This person looks at everything with equal eyes, without favoring one creature over another.
Bhagavad Gita 6.29.keyIdea: Through devoted practice, a yogi perceives a unity: the same essence present in all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 6.29.contextNote: This verse describes a state of perception that comes from yoga practice—not a belief to adopt, but a way of seeing that the text says is possible.

Bhagavad Gita 6.30.simpleEnglish: Someone who sees Krishna in all things, and sees all things in Krishna, never loses Krishna—and Krishna never loses that person. It is a bond that does not break.
Bhagavad Gita 6.30.keyIdea: A person who perceives the divine in everything and everything in the divine stays connected to that divine presence.
Bhagavad Gita 6.30.contextNote: This verse describes a state of spiritual perception. The speaker is Krishna, teaching about what happens when a person's way of seeing the world changes completely.

Bhagavad Gita 6.31.simpleEnglish: A person who worships and honors the divine in all living things, and sees them all as one, stays connected to that divine presence no matter what they are doing in their daily life.
Bhagavad Gita 6.31.keyIdea: Seeing the divine in all beings and all things as one allows a person to stay spiritually connected in every moment.
