Bhagavad Gita 10.36.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching where he describes his presence in different aspects of the world. He is not saying he approves of cheating; he is saying that even in human activities—good and bad—his power shows up.

Bhagavad Gita 10.39.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna: "I am the seed of all living things. Nothing that moves or stays still can exist without me."
Bhagavad Gita 10.39.keyIdea: Krishna claims to be the fundamental source from which all existence arises.
Bhagavad Gita 10.39.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about his divine nature. He is describing himself as the ultimate cause or origin of everything in creation.

Bhagavad Gita 10.38.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: "I am the rod that those who restrain use. I am the policy of those who want victory. I am the silence that keeps secrets safe. I am the knowledge that those with knowledge have."
Bhagavad Gita 10.38.keyIdea: Krishna claims to be present in discipline, strategy, discretion, and wisdom.
Bhagavad Gita 10.38.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's list of his divine manifestations—the ways he appears in the world. He is saying that whenever discipline, winning strategy, wise silence, or true knowledge shows up, his presence is there.

Bhagavad Gita 10.40.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that his divine powers have no end. What he has just shown Arjuna is only a small part of all the powers he has.
Bhagavad Gita 10.40.keyIdea: Krishna's divine powers are endless, and what he revealed was only a sample.
Bhagavad Gita 10.40.contextNote: Krishna has been listing examples of his presence in the world—in nature, in strength, in knowledge. This verse closes that list by saying there is much more he has not mentioned.

Bhagavad Gita 10.37.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: "Among the Vrishni clan (a warrior family), I am Vasudeva (my father's name, used to mean the supreme being). Among the Pandavas (the five brothers in this story), I am Arjuna (the warrior asking questions). Among sages, I am Vyasa (the poet who wrote this epic). Among wise teachers, I am Ushana (a legendary teacher of strategy)."
Bhagavad Gita 10.37.keyIdea: Krishna claims to embody the greatest or most important figure in each group—warrior families, the Pandava brothers, sages, and teachers.
Bhagavad Gita 10.37.contextNote: This is part of Krishna's teaching about his divine nature. He is listing examples across different categories to show his presence in all realms of knowledge and power.

Bhagavad Gita 10.41.simpleEnglish: Anything powerful, glorious, or splendid in the world comes from a portion of Krishna's energy. When you see something great, you are seeing a small part of his power.
Bhagavad Gita 10.41.keyIdea: All greatness and power in the world originates from Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 10.41.contextNote: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna. This verse teaches that whatever we admire as powerful or beautiful is not independent—it is an expression of divine energy.

Bhagavad Gita 11.1.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) says: You have spoken words about the deepest truth—how the supreme soul and the individual soul are related. These words were meant to help me, and now my confusion is gone.
Bhagavad Gita 11.1.keyIdea: Arjuna says that Krishna's teaching has cleared away his confusion.
Bhagavad Gita 11.1.contextNote: This is Arjuna speaking at the start of a new section. He is responding to Krishna's earlier teachings and saying they have helped him understand.

Bhagavad Gita 11.3.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) tells Krishna: "What you have said about yourself is true. I want to see your divine form—the way you really are as the highest lord."
Bhagavad Gita 11.3.keyIdea: Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his true divine nature.
Bhagavad Gita 11.3.contextNote: Arjuna has been listening to Krishna teach him. Now he wants to see Krishna's actual divine form, not just hear about it.

Bhagavad Gita 10.42.simpleEnglish: Krishna says to Arjuna: "Why do you need to know all these details about me? The truth is simpler. I hold up the whole world with just one small part of myself."
Bhagavad Gita 10.42.keyIdea: Krishna suggests that understanding his infinite nature in full detail is less important than grasping one basic fact: he sustains all existence with only a fraction of his power.
Bhagavad Gita 10.42.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has described his many forms and powers. He is now saying that all that detail, while true, misses the main point—his vastness is so great that the entire universe is just a tiny expression of him.

Bhagavad Gita 11.2.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is speaking to Krishna (a divine teacher). He says: "I have heard you explain in detail how all things are created and destroyed. I have also heard about your endless power and greatness."
Bhagavad Gita 11.2.keyIdea: Arjuna acknowledges that Krishna has taught him about creation, destruction, and divine power.
Bhagavad Gita 11.2.contextNote: This verse comes early in the Bhagavad Gita. Arjuna is responding to Krishna's teachings and preparing to ask for something more—a direct vision of Krishna's divine form.
difficultTerms: lotus-eyed (a poetic way to describe Krishna)

Bhagavad Gita 11.4.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is asking Krishna to show him his divine form. Arjuna says: if you think I can see it, then show me your true, endless form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.4.keyIdea: Arjuna asks Krishna to reveal his divine nature.
Bhagavad Gita 11.4.contextNote: Krishna has just told Arjuna that he cannot see Krishna's divine form with ordinary eyes. Now Arjuna asks Krishna to show it anyway, if Krishna believes Arjuna can handle it.

Bhagavad Gita 11.5.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna to look and see his many forms. There are hundreds and thousands of them. Each one is different—different colors, different shapes, all divine.
Bhagavad Gita 11.5.keyIdea: Krishna is showing Arjuna that he has countless divine forms, not just one.
Bhagavad Gita 11.5.contextNote: Arjuna has asked to see Krishna's true nature. This verse is Krishna's response, beginning to reveal his cosmic form.

Bhagavad Gita 11.8.simpleEnglish: Arjuna cannot see Krishna's true form with his ordinary eyes. Krishna gives him a divine eye so he can see it. Now Arjuna can look at Krishna's divine power.
Bhagavad Gita 11.8.keyIdea: To perceive something beyond the ordinary world, a person needs more than ordinary sight.
Bhagavad Gita 11.8.contextNote: Krishna is about to show Arjuna his cosmic form—something vast and overwhelming that human eyes alone cannot take in.

Bhagavad Gita 11.7.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (Gudakesa, "thick-haired one") to look at his body right now. Inside it, Arjuna can see the whole world—everything that moves and everything that stands still—all in one place. Krishna says Arjuna can also see anything else he wants to see.
Bhagavad Gita 11.7.keyIdea: Krishna is showing Arjuna that his divine form contains the entire universe.
Bhagavad Gita 11.7.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's revelation of his cosmic form (Viśvarūpa) to Arjuna. Arjuna has asked to see Krishna's divine nature, and Krishna is inviting him to witness it within his body.

Bhagavad Gita 11.9.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) tells the king: After Krishna spoke those words, he showed Arjuna his supreme divine form—a form beyond the ordinary world.
Bhagavad Gita 11.9.keyIdea: Krishna reveals his divine nature to Arjuna by showing him a form that is not human.
Bhagavad Gita 11.9.contextNote: This verse marks the moment when Krishna stops speaking and begins to show Arjuna something extraordinary. The "supreme divine form" is what Arjuna is about to witness in the verses that follow.

Bhagavad Gita 11.6.simpleEnglish: Krishna is telling Arjuna to look at the divine form he is showing. Arjuna can see many kinds of gods and beings—the Adityas (sun gods), Vasus (gods of natural forces), Rudras (fierce gods), the Asvins (twin gods), and Maruts (wind gods). Arjuna sees wonders he has never seen before.
Bhagavad Gita 11.6.keyIdea: Krishna reveals his cosmic form by showing Arjuna many divine beings at once.
Bhagavad Gita 11.6.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's revelation of his universal form (Viśvarūpa) to Arjuna. The names refer to different classes of gods in Hindu tradition. The point is that Arjuna is witnessing something extraordinary and unprecedented.

Bhagavad Gita 11.10.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees a form with many mouths and many eyes. It has many wonderful sights within it—many divine ornaments and many divine weapons raised up.
Bhagavad Gita 11.10.keyIdea: Arjuna is witnessing Krishna's cosmic form, which is vast and has countless features.
Bhagavad Gita 11.10.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form (Viśvarūpa). The form is described through its many parts and divine qualities.

Bhagavad Gita 11.11.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees a deity wearing flowers and fine clothes, decorated with jewels and perfume. The figure has faces looking in every direction and holds weapons standing upright. Everything about it is full of wonder and seems endless.
Bhagavad Gita 11.11.keyIdea: Arjuna is witnessing a divine form that is vast, beautiful, and all-seeing.
Bhagavad Gita 11.11.contextNote: This verse describes what Arjuna sees when Krishna reveals his divine form. The "faces in all directions" means the deity can see and know everything at once.

Bhagavad Gita 11.12.simpleEnglish: Imagine a thousand suns all shining at the same time in the sky. That brightness would be like the brightness of this mighty being. Arjuna is trying to describe what he sees when Krishna shows him his true form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.12.keyIdea: A comparison: the light of a thousand suns equals the brightness of Krishna's divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.12.contextNote: Krishna has revealed his cosmic form to Arjuna. This verse is part of that vision—Arjuna is using the brightest thing he knows (the sun) to help explain what he is witnessing.

Bhagavad Gita 11.13.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (the son of Pandu) looked at the body of Krishna (the god of gods) and saw the whole universe inside it. Everything was there at once, but also divided into many separate parts.
Bhagavad Gita 11.13.keyIdea: Arjuna witnessed the infinite universe contained within Krishna's divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.13.contextNote: This verse describes a moment in the Bhagavad Gita when Krishna reveals his cosmic form to Arjuna. Arjuna is seeing something beyond the ordinary world—a vision of the divine that holds all existence at once.

Bhagavad Gita 11.14.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (Dhananjaya) is overwhelmed with wonder. His hair stands on end. He bows his head to Krishna and joins his hands together in respect, then speaks.
Bhagavad Gita 11.14.keyIdea: Arjuna's awe at what he has just witnessed moves him to bow and address Krishna with reverence.
Bhagavad Gita 11.14.contextNote: This verse comes right after Krishna has shown Arjuna his cosmic form. Arjuna's physical reaction—hair standing on end, bowing, joined hands—shows how deeply moved he is.

Bhagavad Gita 11.15.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) speaks to Krishna (a god in human form). He says: "I can see inside your body all the gods, all kinds of creatures, Brahman (the creator god) sitting on his lotus throne, and all the wise sages and divine snakes."
Bhagavad Gita 11.15.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses the divine form of Krishna and sees the entire universe contained within it.
Bhagavad Gita 11.15.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has shown Arjuna his cosmic form—a vision of the divine that contains all of existence. Arjuna is describing what he sees in that moment.

Bhagavad Gita 11.16.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is looking at Krishna (a god who has shown his true form). He sees countless arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes everywhere. He cannot find where Krishna ends, where the middle is, or where he begins.
Bhagavad Gita 11.16.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses Krishna's infinite divine form and cannot perceive its boundaries or structure.
Bhagavad Gita 11.16.contextNote: This verse describes what Arjuna sees when Krishna reveals his cosmic form—a vision of something so vast and strange that human sight cannot take it all in or find its limits.

Bhagavad Gita 11.17.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is describing what he sees when Krishna shows him his divine form. Krishna wears a crown and carries a mace and a discus. He shines so brightly on all sides that it is hard to look at him. His light is like a blazing fire or the sun, and it is so great that it cannot be measured or fully understood.
Bhagavad Gita 11.17.keyIdea: Arjuna describes the overwhelming brightness and power of Krishna's divine appearance.
Bhagavad Gita 11.17.contextNote: This is part of the moment when Krishna reveals his true divine form to Arjuna. Arjuna is trying to put into words what he sees, even though it is almost impossible to describe.

Bhagavad Gita 11.19.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) sees Krishna in a cosmic form—without beginning, middle, or end. This form has countless arms, the sun and moon as eyes, and a mouth like blazing fire. Its own light heats the whole universe.
Bhagavad Gita 11.19.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses Krishna as an infinite, all-powerful cosmic being.
Bhagavad Gita 11.19.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's divine form. The description uses impossible, symbolic features to show power and vastness beyond human measure.

Bhagavad Gita 11.18.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (Krishna's student) tells Krishna: You cannot be destroyed. You are the highest thing anyone can know. You hold up the whole universe. You protect what is right and good, forever. I believe you are eternal—you have always existed and always will.
Bhagavad Gita 11.18.keyIdea: Arjuna describes Krishna as indestructible, supreme, and the foundation of all existence.
Bhagavad Gita 11.18.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has seen Krishna's cosmic form (his divine shape that contains all of creation). Arjuna is expressing awe and declaring what he now understands about Krishna's nature.

Bhagavad Gita 11.21.simpleEnglish: The gods are coming into you. Some of them are frightened and praying with their hands pressed together. The great sages and Siddhas (perfected beings) are saying "Be well!" and singing many songs of praise to you.
Bhagavad Gita 11.21.keyIdea: The divine beings respond to the cosmic form with fear, prayer, and praise.
Bhagavad Gita 11.21.contextNote: This verse describes the reaction of gods and sages to Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form. They are entering into it, some in fear, others in reverence.

Bhagavad Gita 11.20.simpleEnglish: The space between heaven and earth, and all directions, are filled by you alone. When the three worlds (the gods' realm, the human realm, and the lower realms) see your wonderful and terrible form, they are frightened.
Bhagavad Gita 11.20.keyIdea: Krishna's cosmic form is so vast and powerful that it fills all space and terrifies all existence.
Bhagavad Gita 11.20.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form in chapter 11. Arjuna is witnessing Krishna reveal his divine nature as the source and sustainer of all worlds.

Bhagavad Gita 11.22.simpleEnglish: Arjuna is seeing Krishna's divine form. Many kinds of beings—gods, spirits, and celestial creatures—are all watching and amazed. They are looking at Krishna in wonder.
Bhagavad Gita 11.22.keyIdea: Many different divine and celestial beings are witnessing Krishna's cosmic form with astonishment.
Bhagavad Gita 11.22.contextNote: This verse lists the names of various classes of beings in Hindu cosmology (Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Siddhas, and others). The point is that all of them—not just Arjuna—are seeing and marveling at Krishna's revelation.

Bhagavad Gita 11.23.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) sees Krishna's true form—a giant shape with many faces, eyes, arms, legs, and stomachs, with fearsome jaws. Arjuna says that all people who see this form are terrified, and he is terrified too.
Bhagavad Gita 11.23.keyIdea: Arjuna describes his fear at witnessing Krishna's vast divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.23.contextNote: Krishna has just revealed his universal form to Arjuna. This verse shows Arjuna's reaction—he is overwhelmed and frightened by what he sees.

Bhagavad Gita 11.24.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) sees Krishna in a cosmic form—huge, touching the sky, shining with many colors, with a wide-open mouth and enormous blazing eyes. The sight terrifies him so much that he loses his courage and cannot find peace.
Bhagavad Gita 11.24.keyIdea: A vision of divine power can overwhelm human fear and composure.
Bhagavad Gita 11.24.contextNote: Arjuna has asked Krishna to show his true form. This verse is Arjuna's reaction to that revelation—he is frightened by what he sees.

Bhagavad Gita 11.25.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees Krishna's cosmic form with terrible mouths full of fangs, burning like the fire of destruction. He cannot tell which direction is which, and he feels no peace. He asks Krishna to be merciful—Krishna, the lord of gods who fills the whole universe.
Bhagavad Gita 11.25.keyIdea: Arjuna is overwhelmed and frightened by the terrifying appearance of Krishna's divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.25.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's reaction to seeing Krishna reveal his cosmic form (Viśvarūpa). The "fire of destruction" refers to the end of time in Hindu cosmology. Arjuna's fear and disorientation show how vast and overwhelming divine power can seem to a human.

Bhagavad Gita 11.27.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees soldiers rushing into Krishna's enormous mouths. The jaws are terrifying and fierce. Some soldiers, their heads crushed, are stuck between the teeth.
Bhagavad Gita 11.27.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses a vision of Krishna's cosmic form consuming warriors in a terrible way.
Bhagavad Gita 11.27.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form (Viśvarūpa). Krishna has revealed his divine nature as the all-consuming force of time and destruction. The image is graphic and meant to show the overwhelming, terrifying power of the divine.

Bhagavad Gita 11.28.simpleEnglish: Just as many rivers flow toward the ocean, so these warriors of the human world are entering your mouths, which blaze all around.
Bhagavad Gita 11.28.keyIdea: The verse compares warriors rushing into Krishna's mouth to rivers flowing toward the sea.
Bhagavad Gita 11.28.contextNote: This is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's cosmic form. The "mouths blazing" refers to the terrifying divine shape Arjuna is seeing.

Bhagavad Gita 11.26.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees all the sons of Dhritarashtra (the blind king whose sons are fighting against Arjuna's family), along with the kings allied with them, and the great warriors Bhishma and Drona, and the charioteer's son, and even Arjuna's own side's best fighters—all of them entering the mouth of Krishna's cosmic form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.26.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses all the armies—enemies and allies alike—being drawn into Krishna's divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.26.contextNote: This verse is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form (Viśvarūpa). Arjuna is naming the key figures he recognizes being consumed by the form. The full verse continues with the image of warriors entering Krishna's mouth and being crushed between his teeth.

Bhagavad Gita 11.29.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees that people are rushing into Krishna's mouths like moths flying into a flame. Just as moths move faster and faster toward the fire and burn up, these people are moving toward their own destruction.
Bhagavad Gita 11.29.keyIdea: The image shows that people are drawn toward Krishna with the same force that moths are drawn to fire—and with the same fatal result.
Bhagavad Gita 11.29.contextNote: This verse comes from Arjuna's vision of Krishna's cosmic form. Krishna is showing Arjuna the nature of time and fate: all beings are moving toward their end, pulled by forces they cannot resist.

Bhagavad Gita 11.30.simpleEnglish: Arjuna sees Krishna's cosmic form with many mouths blazing with fire. The mouths are swallowing and licking all the people around them. The fierce light from Krishna's form fills the whole universe and burns with heat.
Bhagavad Gita 11.30.keyIdea: Arjuna witnesses the terrifying power of Krishna's divine form consuming all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 11.30.contextNote: This is part of Arjuna's vision of Krishna's universal form (Viśvarūpa). The image is frightening and overwhelming—not meant to be gentle or comforting.

Bhagavad Gita 11.31.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) sees Krishna in a terrifying, powerful form. He bows and asks: "Who are you really? Please be kind to me. I want to understand you—the one who was here at the beginning. I don't know what you're doing or why."
Bhagavad Gita 11.31.keyIdea: Arjuna is confused and frightened by Krishna's divine form and asks him to explain himself.
Bhagavad Gita 11.31.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has shown Arjuna a vision of his true divine nature. Arjuna is overwhelmed and doesn't understand what he is seeing.

Bhagavad Gita 11.32.simpleEnglish: Krishna shows Arjuna a vision of himself as time itself—the force that destroys and ends all things. He says he is already at work ending the worlds. All the enemy soldiers standing across the battlefield will die anyway, with or without Arjuna's help.
Bhagavad Gita 11.32.keyIdea: Krishna tells Arjuna that death and destruction are already happening; the enemy's fate is sealed.
Bhagavad Gita 11.32.contextNote: This is part of Krishna's cosmic vision (the Viśvarūpa). Arjuna has asked to see Krishna's true form, and Krishna is showing him something vast and terrifying—himself as time, which destroys everything. The point is not to comfort Arjuna, but to show him that events are already in motion beyond his control.

Bhagavad Gita 11.33.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight. He says Arjuna will win glory and a rich kingdom by defeating his enemies. But Krishna also says he has already killed all these warriors—Arjuna will just be the instrument, like a tool, that carries out what is already decided.
Bhagavad Gita 11.33.keyIdea: Krishna urges Arjuna to fight, telling him the outcome is already set and he is only the means to fulfill it.
Bhagavad Gita 11.33.contextNote: This verse comes near the end of Krishna's long teaching. Arjuna has been troubled about fighting his own relatives. Krishna is now telling him to act, and explaining that the warriors are already "killed"—meaning their fate is sealed, not that Arjuna must feel responsible for choosing their deaths.

Bhagavad Gita 11.34.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that Drona (the weapons teacher), Bhishma (the great warrior), Jayadratha, Karna, and other brave fighters are already dead—Krishna has killed them. Arjuna should kill them too and not be afraid. If Arjuna fights, he will win against his enemies.
Bhagavad Gita 11.34.keyIdea: Krishna tells Arjuna that the enemy warriors are already doomed, so Arjuna should fight without fear.
Bhagavad Gita 11.34.contextNote: This is part of Krishna's vision to Arjuna in Chapter 11. Krishna is showing Arjuna a divine sight of the future or the true nature of events, in which these warriors are already defeated. Krishna urges Arjuna to act without hesitation.

Bhagavad Gita 11.36.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (the warrior) speaks: "It makes sense, Krishna, that the whole world is happy and drawn to you. Demons run away in fear in every direction. And all the Siddhas (perfected beings) bow down to you."
Bhagavad Gita 11.36.keyIdea: Arjuna praises Krishna's power and the effect his presence has on all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 11.36.contextNote: Arjuna has just seen Krishna's cosmic form. This verse is his response—he is saying that Krishna's greatness makes sense now that he has witnessed it.

Bhagavad Gita 11.35.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) said: After hearing Krishna's words, Arjuna trembled with fear. He pressed his palms together in respect, bowed down, and spoke to Krishna again—his voice shaking and his throat tight.
Bhagavad Gita 11.35.keyIdea: Arjuna is overwhelmed and frightened by what Krishna has just shown him.
Bhagavad Gita 11.35.contextNote: This verse describes Arjuna's physical and emotional reaction. He has just witnessed Krishna's cosmic form in the previous verses, which terrified him.

Bhagavad Gita 11.37.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) asks: why should anyone not bow to you? You are greater than Brahman (the creator god), and you made everything. You are the infinite lord of all gods, and you fill the whole universe. You are what cannot be destroyed, what exists, what does not exist, and what lies beyond both.
Bhagavad Gita 11.37.keyIdea: Arjuna describes Krishna as supreme—beyond all gods and all categories of being.
Bhagavad Gita 11.37.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has shown Arjuna his cosmic form (his true divine shape). Arjuna is expressing awe and explaining why everyone should honor Krishna.

Bhagavad Gita 11.38.simpleEnglish: Arjuna is speaking to Krishna. He says: You are the first god, the ancient one. You hold up this whole universe. You know everything, and you are what everything is trying to know. You are the highest goal. Everything in the universe is filled with you, and you have infinite forms.
Bhagavad Gita 11.38.keyIdea: Arjuna declares that Krishna is the ultimate source and support of all existence.
Bhagavad Gita 11.38.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has seen Krishna's cosmic form (the Viśvarūpa). Arjuna is now praising Krishna directly, using titles and descriptions that recognize his supreme nature.

Bhagavad Gita 11.40.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) bows to Krishna from every direction—front, back, and all around. He says Krishna has endless power and glory, and fills everything everywhere. Because Krishna is everywhere, Krishna is everything.
Bhagavad Gita 11.40.keyIdea: Arjuna expresses that Krishna is infinite and present in all places.
Bhagavad Gita 11.40.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has shown Arjuna a cosmic vision of his divine form. Arjuna is responding with reverence and awe.

Bhagavad Gita 11.39.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is speaking to Krishna (a god in human form). He says: You are the wind, you are Yama (the god of death), you are fire, you are Varuna (the god of water), you are the moon, you are Prajapati (the creator of people), and you are the great-grandfather of all. I bow to you again and again, a thousand times over.
Bhagavad Gita 11.39.keyIdea: Arjuna recognizes that Krishna is not just a person, but contains all the major gods and forces of nature.
Bhagavad Gita 11.39.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has asked Krishna to show his true divine form. Arjuna is listing the gods and natural powers he sees in Krishna to express his awe and respect.

Bhagavad Gita 11.41.simpleEnglish: Arjuna is speaking to Krishna. He says: "I called you by your name, or 'friend,' without understanding who you really are. I did not know your true greatness."
Bhagavad Gita 11.41.keyIdea: Arjuna realizes he spoke to Krishna casually because he did not understand Krishna's divine nature.
Bhagavad Gita 11.41.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has seen Krishna's universal form (the Viśvarūpa). Arjuna is now recognizing that he treated Krishna as an equal friend, not knowing Krishna was divine.

Bhagavad Gita 11.42.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior prince) is speaking to Krishna (a divine being). Arjuna says: "If I ever made fun of you or treated you without respect—while we were playing, sleeping, eating, or sitting together, whether alone or with others—I ask your forgiveness. You are beyond measure, and I did not understand who you truly are."
Bhagavad Gita 11.42.keyIdea: Arjuna realizes he has not shown proper respect to Krishna and asks for forgiveness.
Bhagavad Gita 11.42.contextNote: This comes after Krishna has shown Arjuna his divine form. Arjuna is now aware of Krishna's true nature and regrets any casual or disrespectful behavior from their past friendship.

Bhagavad Gita 11.43.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) is speaking to Krishna (a god in human form). He says: You are the father of everything—all living things and all non-living things. You are the greatest teacher and the most worthy of respect. No one is equal to you. No one is greater than you. Your power has no match in all three worlds.
Bhagavad Gita 11.43.keyIdea: Arjuna declares that Krishna is supreme over all creation.
Bhagavad Gita 11.43.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has seen Krishna's cosmic form—a vision of Krishna as the entire universe. Arjuna is expressing awe and reverence at what he has witnessed.

Bhagavad Gita 11.44.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) bows down completely to Krishna (the god he has just seen in his true form). He asks Krishna to forgive him, the way a father forgives his son, a friend forgives a friend, or a husband forgives his wife.
Bhagavad Gita 11.44.keyIdea: Arjuna asks for forgiveness after seeing Krishna's overwhelming divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.44.contextNote: This comes after Arjuna has witnessed Krishna reveal his cosmic form—vast, powerful, and frightening. Arjuna is asking Krishna to show mercy and patience with him as he would with someone he loves.

Bhagavad Gita 11.45.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) has just seen Krishna's divine form—something he never saw before. He is amazed and happy, but also frightened. He asks Krishna to show him his regular form again, and he asks Krishna to be kind to him.
Bhagavad Gita 11.45.keyIdea: Arjuna is overwhelmed by the sight of Krishna's divine power and asks to see his human form instead.
Bhagavad Gita 11.45.contextNote: This verse comes after Krishna has revealed his cosmic form to Arjuna. The divine form is so vast and powerful that it fills Arjuna with both wonder and fear.

Bhagavad Gita 11.46.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) asks Krishna to show himself in a familiar way. He wants to see Krishna wearing a crown and holding a mace and a discus (a spinning weapon). Arjuna asks Krishna to take the form with four arms instead of the thousand arms Krishna is showing him now.
Bhagavad Gita 11.46.keyIdea: Arjuna asks Krishna to return to his usual four-armed form because the infinite form is overwhelming.
Bhagavad Gita 11.46.contextNote: Just before this, Krishna showed Arjuna a cosmic vision—a form so vast it contained all of creation. This verse is Arjuna's response: he is asking Krishna to go back to looking like the Krishna he knows.

Bhagavad Gita 11.47.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that he is pleased with him and has shown him a special form using his own power. This form is full of light, spreads everywhere, has no end, and existed from the beginning. No one else has ever seen it before—only Arjuna.
Bhagavad Gita 11.47.keyIdea: Krishna reveals that the cosmic form he showed Arjuna is unique and has never been seen by anyone else.
Bhagavad Gita 11.47.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has seen Krishna's vast cosmic form. Krishna is explaining what Arjuna has just witnessed and why he was given this rare sight.

Bhagavad Gita 11.48.simpleEnglish: Krishna is showing Arjuna a divine form that no one else can see. Not through studying the Vedas (the oldest Hindu texts), not through sacrifices or gifts, not through actions or hard penances—only Arjuna can see this form, and only because Krishna has given him the ability.
Bhagavad Gita 11.48.keyIdea: This divine vision is a gift given only to Arjuna; it cannot be earned through ordinary religious practices.
Bhagavad Gita 11.48.contextNote: Krishna has just revealed his cosmic form to Arjuna. This verse explains that such a vision is not something anyone can achieve through effort or discipline alone—it comes as a direct gift from the divine.

Bhagavad Gita 11.49.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna not to be upset or confused by the frightening form he has just shown him. He asks Arjuna to calm down, feel glad in his heart, and look at that same form again.
Bhagavad Gita 11.49.keyIdea: Krishna reassures Arjuna after revealing a terrifying divine vision.
Bhagavad Gita 11.49.contextNote: Arjuna has just seen Krishna's universal form—vast, many-armed, and overwhelming. This verse is Krishna's immediate response, asking him not to fear what he has witnessed.

Bhagavad Gita 11.51.simpleEnglish: Arjuna (a warrior in the story) says to Krishna: "Now that I see your gentle, human form, my mind is calm again. I have come back to myself."
Bhagavad Gita 11.51.keyIdea: Arjuna recovers his composure after seeing Krishna return to his ordinary appearance.
Bhagavad Gita 11.51.contextNote: Just before this, Krishna showed Arjuna a terrifying cosmic vision of himself. Now Krishna has taken back his normal human shape, and Arjuna's fear has passed.

Bhagavad Gita 11.50.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) tells us: After Krishna spoke to Arjuna, he showed his true form again. Then Krishna took on a gentle, peaceful shape and comforted Arjuna, who was afraid.
Bhagavad Gita 11.50.keyIdea: Krishna returns to his familiar form to calm Arjuna's fear after revealing his cosmic self.
Bhagavad Gita 11.50.contextNote: This verse closes the vision of Krishna's universal form. Arjuna has just seen something overwhelming—Krishna's infinite, all-powerful nature. Now Krishna becomes gentle again so Arjuna can recover.

Bhagavad Gita 11.52.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna: "You have just seen a form of me that is very hard to see. Even the gods (divine beings) always want to see this form, but they cannot easily get to see it."
Bhagavad Gita 11.52.keyIdea: Arjuna has been given a rare sight that even the gods desire.
Bhagavad Gita 11.52.contextNote: This verse comes after Arjuna has witnessed Krishna's cosmic form—a vision of Krishna's divine nature that shows his power and vastness. Krishna is telling Arjuna how special this moment is.

Bhagavad Gita 11.53.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that the form Arjuna just saw cannot be reached through the usual paths—not through studying the Vedas (the oldest Hindu scriptures), not through penance, not through giving gifts, and not through sacrifice. Arjuna saw it in a different way.
Bhagavad Gita 11.53.keyIdea: The divine form Arjuna witnessed is beyond what ordinary spiritual practices can reveal.
Bhagavad Gita 11.53.contextNote: Arjuna has just seen Krishna's cosmic form—a vision of Krishna as the universal divine. This verse explains that such a vision is not earned through the standard religious methods.

Bhagavad Gita 11.54.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that the only way to truly know him, see him, and become one with him is through exclusive devotion—giving your whole heart to him alone, without dividing your attention.
Bhagavad Gita 11.54.keyIdea: Exclusive devotion is the path to truly know and unite with the divine.
Bhagavad Gita 11.54.contextNote: This verse comes at the end of Krishna's revelation of his cosmic form. He is saying that intellectual knowledge or ritual alone cannot bring understanding—only single-minded devotion can.

Bhagavad Gita 11.55.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna (the son of Pandu) about a person who reaches him: someone who does work for Krishna, who sees Krishna as the highest goal, who is devoted to Krishna, who is not attached to rewards, and who feels no hatred toward any living being.
Bhagavad Gita 11.55.keyIdea: A person reaches Krishna through devotion, right action, freedom from attachment, and goodwill toward all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 11.55.contextNote: This verse describes the qualities of someone who achieves union with Krishna. It combines action, devotion, detachment, and universal compassion.

Bhagavad Gita 12.2.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: People who worship him with their whole mind fixed on him, who do this all the time, and who have the strongest faith—these are the ones he thinks are most devoted to him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.2.keyIdea: Constant worship with complete focus and strong faith is what Krishna calls the highest devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 12.2.contextNote: This verse describes what Krishna values in a worshipper. It is part of a teaching about different paths to him.

Bhagavad Gita 12.1.simpleEnglish: Arjuna asks Krishna: Some people worship you constantly and with full attention. Others meditate on something that cannot be seen or destroyed. Which group understands devotion better?
Bhagavad Gita 12.1.keyIdea: Arjuna asks which path of devotion is superior: worshipping a personal god or meditating on the formless, eternal reality.
Bhagavad Gita 12.1.contextNote: This is the opening of Chapter 12. Arjuna is asking Krishna to compare two ways of spiritual practice: devotion to Krishna as a person, and devotion to an abstract, unchanging principle.

Bhagavad Gita 12.3.simpleEnglish: Some people meditate on something that has no form and cannot be described—something that is everywhere, unchanging, and beyond thought. They keep their senses calm and their mind steady and equal toward all things.
Bhagavad Gita 12.3.keyIdea: This verse describes one way to practice meditation: focusing on the formless, unchanging reality that exists everywhere.
Bhagavad Gita 12.3.contextNote: Krishna is contrasting different paths of devotion. This verse describes those who meditate on the abstract, formless aspect of reality rather than on a personal deity.

Bhagavad Gita 12.4.simpleEnglish: People who control their senses and keep the same calm mind everywhere, and who care about the good of all living things, reach Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 12.4.keyIdea: Controlling the senses, staying calm, and caring for all beings leads to Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 12.4.contextNote: This verse describes a path: steady discipline of the senses, an even mind, and devotion to the welfare of all creatures.

Bhagavad Gita 12.5.simpleEnglish: When someone's mind is attached to something they cannot see or perceive, they face greater difficulty. The unperceived path is hard for people who have bodies.
Bhagavad Gita 12.5.keyIdea: Trying to reach something you cannot perceive or understand is harder than following a clear path.
Bhagavad Gita 12.5.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about different paths to him. He is saying that the path of worshipping the formless, unperceived Brahman (ultimate reality) is more difficult than other paths, especially for people bound to the physical world.

Bhagavad Gita 12.6.simpleEnglish: People who give all their work to Krishna, who focus only on him, and who worship him by thinking of him constantly—they reach him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.6.keyIdea: Devotion that gives everything and thinks only of Krishna leads to reaching him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.6.contextNote: This verse describes one path to Krishna: complete surrender of all actions and single-minded devotion through meditation and worship.

Bhagavad Gita 12.8.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna to put his mind on Krishna alone and fix his understanding there too. If you do this, Krishna says, you will live in Krishna—and there is no doubt about it.
Bhagavad Gita 12.8.keyIdea: Krishna teaches that focusing your mind and understanding on him leads to living in him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.8.contextNote: This verse is Krishna's instruction to Arjuna on how to reach him. "Dwell in me" means a state of being united with or absorbed in Krishna.

Bhagavad Gita 12.7.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: "Those who give all their actions to me, who see me as their highest goal, and who worship me with their whole mind fixed only on me—I will quickly rescue them from the ocean of death and rebirth."
Bhagavad Gita 12.7.keyIdea: Krishna promises swift rescue to those who dedicate themselves completely to him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.7.contextNote: This verse describes a condition and a promise. The condition is complete devotion and dedication; the promise is that Krishna will deliver them from the cycle of death and rebirth (saṁsāra).

Bhagavad Gita 12.9.simpleEnglish: If you cannot keep your mind steady on Krishna, then try another way: practice meditation over and over. Through this steady practice, you can reach him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.9.keyIdea: When direct focus is hard, regular practice of meditation can work instead.
Bhagavad Gita 12.9.contextNote: Krishna is offering a second path. The first path (in earlier verses) asks for steady devotion. This verse says: if that is too difficult, use disciplined practice.

Bhagavad Gita 12.10.simpleEnglish: If you cannot do meditation, then make doing work for Krishna your highest goal. Even if you just do actions for Krishna's sake, you will reach perfection.
Bhagavad Gita 12.10.keyIdea: There are different paths to perfection; if meditation is too hard, devoted action is another way.
Bhagavad Gita 12.10.contextNote: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna. This verse offers an alternative path when the listener feels unable to follow a harder practice.

Bhagavad Gita 12.11.simpleEnglish: If you cannot do the practice Krishna described before, then turn to devotion to him. With self-control, give up wanting the results of your actions.
Bhagavad Gita 12.11.keyIdea: When a spiritual practice feels too hard, devotion and letting go of results can be a simpler path.
Bhagavad Gita 12.11.contextNote: This verse is Krishna's third option for Arjuna. He has already offered two paths; this one is for those who find even those too difficult.

Bhagavad Gita 12.12.simpleEnglish: Knowledge is better than just practicing meditation over and over. Concentration (focusing the mind deeply) is better than knowledge alone. But giving up the desire for rewards from your actions is better still. When you stop wanting rewards, peace comes naturally.
Bhagavad Gita 12.12.keyIdea: A path of deepening practice: from meditation to knowledge to concentration to letting go of rewards—and peace follows.
Bhagavad Gita 12.12.contextNote: Krishna is describing a progression, each step building on the last. The final step—not caring about rewards—leads to inner peace.

Bhagavad Gita 12.14.simpleEnglish: A person who is content, always devoted to practice, controls their own mind, and holds firm decisions is dear to Krishna. If their mind and understanding are turned toward Krishna, that person is loved by him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.14.keyIdea: Krishna describes the person he loves: someone content, disciplined, steady, and devoted.
Bhagavad Gita 12.14.contextNote: This verse lists qualities Krishna values in a devoted person. It is part of Krishna's teaching about different paths to him.

Bhagavad Gita 12.13.simpleEnglish: A person devoted to Krishna does not hate any living thing. They are friendly and kind to others. They do not think "this is mine" or feel proud about themselves. Happiness and sadness affect them equally. They forgive people.
Bhagavad Gita 12.13.keyIdea: A devoted person treats all beings without hatred, stays humble, and remains calm through both joy and sorrow.
Bhagavad Gita 12.13.contextNote: This verse describes qualities that Krishna values in a devoted follower. It is part of a longer teaching about devotion.

Bhagavad Gita 12.15.simpleEnglish: A person who does not disturb the world, and whom the world does not disturb, is dear to Krishna. This person is free from joy, anger, fear, and agitation.
Bhagavad Gita 12.15.keyIdea: A person who remains calm and does not upset others, and is not upset by them, is valued.
Bhagavad Gita 12.15.contextNote: Krishna is describing a quality he values in a person—not causing trouble and not being thrown off balance by trouble.

Bhagavad Gita 12.16.simpleEnglish: Krishna describes a person he holds dear: someone who does not worry about what others think, keeps themselves clean and honest, works hard, stays calm and fair, and does not cling to the rewards of their actions. This person gives up the desire to control what comes from what they do.
Bhagavad Gita 12.16.keyIdea: A person who acts without attachment to results, stays balanced, and does not seek reward is beloved by Krishna.
Bhagavad Gita 12.16.contextNote: The verse lists qualities that Krishna values in a devotee. "Abandons all actions" means letting go of the wish to own or control the fruits of one's work, not stopping work itself.

Bhagavad Gita 12.17.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: the person who is devoted to me, who does not get excited by good things or upset by bad things, who does not grieve or crave, and who lets go of both what feels pleasant and what feels unpleasant—that person is dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.17.keyIdea: Devotion to Krishna includes a kind of inner balance where you do not swing between joy and sorrow, desire and aversion.
Bhagavad Gita 12.17.contextNote: This verse describes a quality of the devoted person: they remain steady and unshaken by the ups and downs of life. It is not about being cold or uncaring, but about not being pulled around by likes and dislikes.

Bhagavad Gita 12.18.simpleEnglish: A person who treats friends and enemies the same way, who feels the same about praise and blame, who stays calm in cold and heat, pleasure and pain—this person has let go of clinging to things.
Bhagavad Gita 12.18.keyIdea: Evenness of mind means not being shaken by what happens around you or to you.
Bhagavad Gita 12.18.contextNote: This verse describes a quality called *samatva* (evenness). It is not indifference or not caring; it is a steady mind that does not swing between extremes.

Bhagavad Gita 12.19.simpleEnglish: Krishna describes a person he loves: someone who treats praise and blame the same way, speaks little, feels satisfied with whatever comes, has no fixed home, keeps a steady mind, and is full of devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 12.19.keyIdea: Krishna values a person who is unmoved by praise or blame and devoted to him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.19.contextNote: This verse lists qualities that Krishna says make a person dear to him. It is part of a teaching about different paths and types of devotion.

Bhagavad Gita 12.20.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: people who trust deeply, follow the sacred path described here, and see me as their highest goal are very dear to him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.20.keyIdea: Devotion combined with faith and seeing Krishna as the ultimate goal makes someone precious to him.
Bhagavad Gita 12.20.contextNote: This verse comes at the end of Krishna's teaching on devotion. He is saying that those who practice what he has taught—with real faith and with him as their center—are closest to his heart.

Bhagavad Gita 13.1.simpleEnglish: Arjuna asks Krishna to explain two things: nature and the person, the field and the one who knows the field. He wants to understand knowledge itself and what can be known.
Bhagavad Gita 13.1.keyIdea: Arjuna is asking Krishna to teach him about the difference between the physical world and the conscious being who experiences it.
Bhagavad Gita 13.1.contextNote: This is the start of a teaching section. "Field" (kshetra) means the body and the physical world. "The one who knows the field" (kshetragna) means the conscious self or awareness inside it. Arjuna wants to understand this distinction.

Bhagavad Gita 13.2.simpleEnglish: Krishna tells Arjuna that this body is called a "field" (kṣhetra). Whoever knows this field is called the "knower of the field" (kṣhetra-jña). Krishna says he is the knower of the field in all fields.
Bhagavad Gita 13.2.keyIdea: The body is described as a field, and there is a knower who understands it.
Bhagavad Gita 13.2.contextNote: This verse introduces an important teaching: the body and mind are like a field, and there is a conscious knower separate from that field. The verse sets up the idea that understanding this distinction is central to the teaching of Chapter 13.

Bhagavad Gita 13.5.simpleEnglish: Wise teachers have explained this knowledge in many different ways. They used different kinds of poetry and logical arguments to make it clear.
Bhagavad Gita 13.5.keyIdea: The same spiritual truth has been taught by many teachers using different methods and words.
Bhagavad Gita 13.5.contextNote: This verse introduces the idea that sacred knowledge can be understood through many paths—poetry, logic, and reasoning all point toward the same truth.

Bhagavad Gita 13.3.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: I think the most important knowledge is understanding two things—the field (kṣhetra, the body and the world around it) and the knower of the field (kṣhetra-jña, the conscious being inside). Now I will explain what the field is, what it is like, how it changes, where it comes from, and who the knower is and what powers he has.
Bhagavad Gita 13.3.keyIdea: True knowledge means understanding both the physical world and the conscious being that experiences it.
Bhagavad Gita 13.3.contextNote: This verse opens Chapter 13, where Krishna begins to teach about the difference between matter (the field) and spirit (the knower of the field). The "field" is the body and everything material; the "knower" is the eternal conscious self.

Bhagavad Gita 13.4.simpleEnglish: Sages have sung about this field and the knower in many different ways. They wrote it in hymns and texts full of careful reasoning. Now Krishna will explain it briefly to Arjuna.
Bhagavad Gita 13.4.keyIdea: The teachings about the field and the knower come from many ancient sources, and now Krishna will give a short version.
Bhagavad Gita 13.4.contextNote: This verse introduces Krishna's explanation. He is saying that wise teachers have already written about these ideas in many forms, and he will now summarize them.

Bhagavad Gita 13.6.simpleEnglish: The field (kshetra) includes the five great elements, ego, intellect, and the unmanifest nature. It also includes the ten senses and the five objects of sense—desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body, and consciousness. These things together make up the field that changes.
Bhagavad Gita 13.6.keyIdea: Krishna lists what makes up the "field"—the body and mind and all their parts and experiences.
Bhagavad Gita 13.6.contextNote: In Chapter 13, Krishna teaches Arjuna about the "field" (kshetra) and the "knower of the field" (kshetrajna). This verse names the parts of the field—everything that is physical or mental and subject to change.

Bhagavad Gita 13.7.simpleEnglish: This verse lists qualities that make up the "field" (the body and mind where knowledge grows). They include: not being vain, not showing off, not hurting others, forgiving people, being honest, respecting a teacher, staying pure, being steady, and holding back from doing whatever you want.
Bhagavad Gita 13.7.keyIdea: The verse describes inner qualities as the ground where wisdom can take root.
Bhagavad Gita 13.7.contextNote: Krishna is explaining what he means by "the field"—not just the body, but the character and habits that shape how a person thinks and learns.

Bhagavad Gita 13.8.simpleEnglish: The verse lists qualities of wisdom: not seeking honor, not pretending to be what you are not, not harming others, patience, honesty, respect for teachers, cleanliness, steadiness, and control over your own mind and senses. It also includes understanding that birth, aging, sickness, and death are real parts of life.
Bhagavad Gita 13.8.keyIdea: Wisdom shows itself through humility, truthfulness, self-control, and clear sight of how life actually works.
Bhagavad Gita 13.8.contextNote: This verse is part of a longer teaching about what knowledge and wisdom look like in practice. Krishna is describing the marks of a person who understands reality.

Bhagavad Gita 13.11.simpleEnglish: Steady devotion to the supreme—without turning away—is real knowledge. It means living apart from crowds and having no interest in social gatherings. Anything that goes against this understanding is called ignorance.
Bhagavad Gita 13.11.keyIdea: True knowledge is unwavering devotion to understanding the connection between the individual self and the supreme; ignorance is the opposite.
Bhagavad Gita 13.11.contextNote: This verse describes what counts as knowledge and what counts as ignorance in the teaching of the Gita. It emphasizes single-minded focus and withdrawal from worldly distractions.

Bhagavad Gita 13.9.simpleEnglish: Not clinging to what your senses want. Not thinking "this is mine" about your family or home. Staying calm and even when good things and bad things come your way.
Bhagavad Gita 13.9.keyIdea: Wisdom means letting go of attachment and staying balanced through life's ups and downs.
Bhagavad Gita 13.9.contextNote: This verse lists qualities that show a person has real knowledge. It is not saying you must stop loving your family—it is describing a way of being that does not depend on things staying the way you want.

Bhagavad Gita 13.10.simpleEnglish: A person who practices wisdom stays unattached to children, spouse, and home. They keep the same calm mind whether things go well or badly. They avoid crowds and prefer clean, quiet places.
Bhagavad Gita 13.10.keyIdea: Wisdom comes with detachment from family ties and an even mind in all circumstances.
Bhagavad Gita 13.10.contextNote: This verse describes the outer signs and inner qualities of someone who is learning to see beyond the material world. It is not saying family is bad—it is saying that clinging to them as the center of life clouds understanding.

Bhagavad Gita 13.12.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he will teach what is worth knowing. When you understand this, you reach a state beyond death. It is the highest Brahman (the ultimate reality)—it has no beginning and no end, and it cannot be called simply real or unreal.
Bhagavad Gita 13.12.keyIdea: The highest knowledge is about Brahman, which is beyond ordinary categories of existence.
Bhagavad Gita 13.12.contextNote: This verse introduces a teaching about what true knowledge is. Brahman is described in a way that goes beyond how we normally describe things—it is not bound by time and cannot be sorted into simple "is" or "is not" categories.

Bhagavad Gita 13.13.simpleEnglish: I will now explain what you should know. When you truly understand this, you reach immortality. It is the eternal Brahman (the ultimate reality), without beginning. It is neither being nor non-being—it cannot be described in ordinary terms.
Bhagavad Gita 13.13.keyIdea: The ultimate reality is beyond ordinary categories of existence and non-existence.
Bhagavad Gita 13.13.contextNote: This verse introduces a teaching about Brahman. The Sanskrit describes something that cannot fit into normal ideas of "real" or "unreal"—it points to something beyond everyday understanding.

Bhagavad Gita 13.14.simpleEnglish: The supreme being has all the powers of the senses but is not bound by any of them. It is not attached to anything, yet it supports everything. It has no qualities of its own, yet it experiences all qualities.
Bhagavad Gita 13.14.keyIdea: The ultimate reality is beyond the senses and qualities, yet present everywhere and in everything.
Bhagavad Gita 13.14.contextNote: This verse describes a paradox: something that has all powers but uses none, that supports all things while remaining untouched by them. It is trying to point to something beyond ordinary experience.

Bhagavad Gita 13.16.simpleEnglish: The divine reality (called Brahman) is present everywhere—inside and outside all living things. It is so fine and subtle that we cannot see it or know it directly. Yet it holds everything up and makes everything happen.
Bhagavad Gita 13.16.keyIdea: One reality pervades all things, though it remains invisible and beyond ordinary knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 13.16.contextNote: This verse describes how the ultimate reality is both near and far, both inside and outside, yet unified. It is the ground of all existence.

Bhagavad Gita 13.17.simpleEnglish: This verse describes something that is not divided into separate parts, yet appears to be spread throughout all living things. It is the sustainer of all beings. It is knowledge itself, the thing being known, and the way to reach understanding. It is placed in the heart of everything.
Bhagavad Gita 13.17.keyIdea: The verse describes an underlying reality that is both unified and present everywhere, and is the source of all knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 13.17.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about the nature of ultimate reality (Brahman). The "it" refers to the eternal principle that Krishna has been describing—something beyond the physical world that sustains all existence.

Bhagavad Gita 13.15.simpleEnglish: The Supreme Self (the deepest reality) appears in all the senses and their qualities, yet it is separate from them. It is unattached, it supports all beings, and it has no qualities of its own—yet it experiences all qualities. It is so subtle that it cannot be known through ordinary understanding; it is both far away and near at hand.
Bhagavad Gita 13.15.keyIdea: The Supreme Self is present everywhere and in everything, yet remains untouched and beyond ordinary knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 13.15.contextNote: This verse describes the nature of the Supreme Self (Brahman) in paradoxical terms—present yet separate, knowable yet unknowable. It is meant to show that ultimate reality cannot be grasped by the senses or ordinary thought alone.

Bhagavad Gita 13.19.simpleEnglish: Krishna has explained the field (the body and mind) and knowledge about it. A person devoted to Krishna who understands this teaching comes to share Krishna's nature.
Bhagavad Gita 13.19.keyIdea: Understanding the field and knowledge leads a devoted person toward Krishna's nature.
Bhagavad Gita 13.19.contextNote: This verse concludes Krishna's teaching about the field and knowledge. "Sharing Krishna's nature" means becoming like him—not literally becoming Krishna, but moving toward his qualities.

Bhagavad Gita 13.18.simpleEnglish: The light of all lights, beyond darkness—that is knowledge. Knowledge, what can be known, and the path to knowing are all placed in the heart of everyone. Krishna says: when a person understands this, they become ready to join with me.
Bhagavad Gita 13.18.keyIdea: Knowledge of the true self is the light that dispels ignorance, and it lives within all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 13.18.contextNote: This verse wraps up Krishna's teaching about the field (the body and mind), the knower of the field (the self), and knowledge itself. He is saying that understanding these three things is the path to unity with him.

Bhagavad Gita 13.20.simpleEnglish: Nature (prakṛiti) is what gives the body and senses their power to act. Spirit (puruṣha) is what makes it possible to feel pleasure and pain. Both have always existed.
Bhagavad Gita 13.20.keyIdea: The verse teaches that nature and spirit are two separate things: one makes action possible, the other makes experience possible.
Bhagavad Gita 13.20.contextNote: This verse is part of a teaching about what nature and spirit are. It does not say which is better or what a person should do about them.

Bhagavad Gita 13.22.simpleEnglish: The person living in nature experiences the qualities that come from nature. The reason this person is born into good or bad situations is that they are attached to those qualities.
Bhagavad Gita 13.22.keyIdea: A person's attachment to nature's qualities determines what kind of life they are born into.
Bhagavad Gita 13.22.contextNote: This verse teaches that our circumstances are not random—they follow from what we are attached to. The "qualities" (guṇas) are the three basic forces in nature: purity, passion, and darkness.

Bhagavad Gita 13.21.simpleEnglish: Nature (prakṛiti) is the cause of action and the things that happen. The person (puruṣha) is the one who experiences pleasure and pain. When the person is joined with nature's qualities, that connection is what causes the person to be born into different situations—good or difficult.
Bhagavad Gita 13.21.keyIdea: Nature drives what happens; the person experiences it. Their connection to nature's qualities shapes their circumstances.
Bhagavad Gita 13.21.contextNote: This verse explains a teaching about two principles: nature as the active force, and the person as the experiencer. Their link determines the person's birth and life conditions.

Bhagavad Gita 13.23.simpleEnglish: The supreme spirit (Paramatman) in the body is called the witness, the permitter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, and the great lord. When a person truly understands nature, spirit, and the qualities that make up the world, they are not born again.
Bhagavad Gita 13.23.keyIdea: Understanding the difference between nature, spirit, and the qualities leads to freedom from rebirth.
Bhagavad Gita 13.23.contextNote: This verse describes the supreme spirit's role and teaches that knowledge of these three things—nature, spirit, and qualities—brings liberation.

Bhagavad Gita 13.24.simpleEnglish: A person who truly understands the self and nature—and how they work together through all the qualities—does not take birth again, no matter what they do in the world.
Bhagavad Gita 13.24.keyIdea: Understanding the self and nature deeply means you escape the cycle of rebirth.
Bhagavad Gita 13.24.contextNote: This verse teaches that real knowledge of the self and the natural world brings freedom from being born again and again. It is the goal of spiritual practice in the Gita.

Bhagavad Gita 13.25.simpleEnglish: Some people see the self through meditation. Others study philosophy or practice yoga. Still others follow the path of action. All of them, if they listen carefully to teaching and stay devoted to it, can cross beyond death.
Bhagavad Gita 13.25.keyIdea: Different paths—meditation, study, yoga, and action—all lead to the same goal if followed with devotion and good teaching.
Bhagavad Gita 13.25.contextNote: This verse describes different ways people seek understanding of the self. "Crossing beyond death" means reaching a state beyond ordinary life and its limits.

Bhagavad Gita 13.26.simpleEnglish: Some people don't know this teaching. They hear it from others and worship based on what they've heard. Even they cross over death—because they are devoted to what they have heard.
Bhagavad Gita 13.26.keyIdea: Even those who follow teachings secondhand, without full understanding, can still reach liberation through devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 13.26.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about different paths to understanding reality. He is saying that devotion to the teachings—even when learned indirectly—has real power.
difficultTerms: mṛityuṁ (death, or the cycle of rebirth)

Bhagavad Gita 13.28.simpleEnglish: Someone who sees the divine (the supreme power) present equally in all living things does not harm themselves. That person reaches the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 13.28.keyIdea: Seeing the divine equally in all beings leads to not harming yourself and reaching the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 13.28.contextNote: The verse teaches that recognizing a universal divine presence in all creatures naturally prevents self-harm and leads to spiritual fulfillment.

Bhagavad Gita 13.29.simpleEnglish: A person who truly sees understands that nature does all the actions everywhere. That person also sees that the self is not the one doing them. When someone sees this way, they reach the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 13.29.keyIdea: True understanding means seeing that nature acts, not the self.
Bhagavad Gita 13.29.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of seeing the world. It says that if you understand that actions come from nature (not from your inner self), you can reach a higher state.

Bhagavad Gita 13.30.simpleEnglish: When someone sees that all actions happen through nature, not through a separate "self" doing them, they see truly. They understand that the inner self is not the doer.
Bhagavad Gita 13.30.keyIdea: The real self does not act; nature does all the acting.
Bhagavad Gita 13.30.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of seeing: actions belong to the natural world, not to the inner witness. This understanding is part of the path to wisdom in the Gita.

Bhagavad Gita 13.27.simpleEnglish: Whatever living thing exists—still or moving—comes from the connection between the field (the body) and the one who knows the field (the self). The person who truly sees understands this: the supreme lord is present in all beings equally, and is not destroyed when bodies are destroyed.
Bhagavad Gita 13.27.keyIdea: True seeing means recognizing that one supreme presence inhabits all living things and remains unchanged when individual bodies die.
Bhagavad Gita 13.27.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of understanding reality: that beneath the diversity of all living forms—plants, animals, humans—there is one unchanging presence. The "field" and "one who knows the field" are concepts from earlier in chapter 13 that describe the body and the eternal self.

Bhagavad Gita 13.31.simpleEnglish: When a person sees that all separate things come from one source and spread out from that one place, they understand Brahman (the ultimate reality). At that moment, they reach Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 13.31.keyIdea: Understanding that all separate things come from one source leads to knowing Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 13.31.contextNote: This verse teaches a way of seeing the world: instead of looking at many different things, look for the one source they all come from. That shift in understanding is what it means to "reach" or know Brahman.

Bhagavad Gita 13.32.simpleEnglish: Space is everywhere, but nothing sticks to it or taints it. In the same way, the self (ātman) is in every body, but nothing can taint or touch it.
Bhagavad Gita 13.32.keyIdea: The self is untouched by what happens in the body, just as space cannot be stained.
Bhagavad Gita 13.32.contextNote: This verse uses a comparison to explain that the self remains pure and unaffected, even though it is present in the physical body.

Bhagavad Gita 13.33.simpleEnglish: Just as space is everywhere but does not get stained by anything, the self (ātmā) lives in every body but is not affected by what the body does. The self is like the sun—it shines on everything without being changed by any of it.
Bhagavad Gita 13.33.keyIdea: The self is present everywhere in the body but remains untouched by the body's actions and nature.
Bhagavad Gita 13.33.contextNote: This verse uses two images—space and the sun—to explain how the self can be in all things without being harmed or changed by them. It is part of a teaching about the difference between the body and the self.

Bhagavad Gita 14.1.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he will teach the highest knowledge. This is the best kind of knowledge there is. When sages learn it, they reach the highest perfection and go beyond the limits of the body.
Bhagavad Gita 14.1.keyIdea: Krishna is about to teach a supreme form of knowledge that leads sages to ultimate perfection.
Bhagavad Gita 14.1.contextNote: This verse opens Chapter 14. Krishna is promising to share something he calls the "highest knowledge"—the best of all kinds of knowledge. He says that sages (wise people) who understand it reach perfection and transcend the body.

Bhagavad Gita 14.2.simpleEnglish: People who understand this knowledge and become like Krishna in their nature do not get born when the universe is created. They are not troubled when the universe is destroyed.
Bhagavad Gita 14.2.keyIdea: Understanding this knowledge frees a person from the cycle of creation and destruction.
Bhagavad Gita 14.2.contextNote: The verse speaks of a spiritual state where someone reaches "assimilation with Krishna's essence"—a condition beyond the ordinary cycle of birth and death that affects all other beings.

Bhagavad Gita 14.3.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: "The great Brahman (the ultimate reality) is like a womb for me. I place the seed of life in it. From that comes the birth of all living things, O descendant of Bharata (Arjuna)."
Bhagavad Gita 14.3.keyIdea: Krishna describes how all living beings come into existence through the union of the divine and the material reality.
Bhagavad Gita 14.3.contextNote: This verse uses the image of a seed and womb to explain how creation happens. It is part of Krishna's teaching about the three gunas (qualities of nature) and how all beings arise.

Bhagavad Gita 14.4.simpleEnglish: All living bodies are born from different kinds of wombs. Krishna says the great Brahman (the material nature of the universe) is the main womb, and he is the father who gives the seed. This means all life comes from both matter and spirit working together.
Bhagavad Gita 14.4.keyIdea: All living things come from both material nature and a spiritual source.
Bhagavad Gita 14.4.contextNote: Krishna is explaining how creation works—matter provides the body, and spirit provides the life force. Both are needed.

Bhagavad Gita 14.5.simpleEnglish: Nature has three qualities: goodness, passion, and darkness. These three qualities bind the eternal soul to the body. Krishna is speaking to Arjuna (a warrior) about how these forces work in the world.
Bhagavad Gita 14.5.keyIdea: The three qualities of nature tie the soul to physical life.
Bhagavad Gita 14.5.contextNote: This verse introduces the three gunas (qualities). They are not good or bad in themselves—they are the basic forces that make up all of nature and keep the soul attached to the body.

Bhagavad Gita 14.6.simpleEnglish: Of the three qualities (sattva, rajas, and tamas), goodness is pure and brings light and freedom from pain. But it still binds the soul—through the bonds of pleasure and knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 14.6.keyIdea: Goodness is the purest quality, but it can still trap the soul through attachment to pleasure and learning.
Bhagavad Gita 14.6.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about the three qualities of nature. Even the highest quality, goodness, creates attachment if the soul clings to it.

Bhagavad Gita 14.7.simpleEnglish: Passion (rajas) comes from wanting things and holding on to them. It ties a person to their actions and keeps them caught in the cycle of doing and getting results.
Bhagavad Gita 14.7.keyIdea: Passion binds us through craving and attachment.
Bhagavad Gita 14.7.contextNote: Krishna is describing one of three qualities (gunas) that make up all nature. Here he explains how the quality of passion works—it creates desire, which leads to action, which creates more desire.

Bhagavad Gita 14.8.simpleEnglish: Tamas (a quality of dullness and confusion) comes from not knowing. It clouds the mind of every living being. Heedlessness, laziness, and sleep tie a person down in this state.
Bhagavad Gita 14.8.keyIdea: Tamas, born from ignorance, keeps people trapped through carelessness, laziness, and sleep.
Bhagavad Gita 14.8.contextNote: This verse describes one of three qualities (gunas) that the Gita says make up all things. Tamas is the quality of darkness, heaviness, and confusion—the opposite of clarity and action.

Bhagavad Gita 14.9.simpleEnglish: The three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) each pull a person in a different direction. Goodness connects you with happiness. Passion connects you with action and work. Darkness connects you with carelessness—it hides knowledge and makes you ignore what you should know.
Bhagavad Gita 14.9.keyIdea: Each of the three qualities of nature leads to a different state of mind and behavior.
Bhagavad Gita 14.9.contextNote: This verse describes how sattva (goodness), rajas (passion), and tamas (darkness) are three fundamental qualities that shape how a person thinks and acts. The verse is part of Krishna's teaching about the nature of reality.

Bhagavad Gita 14.10.simpleEnglish: When passion and darkness are held back, goodness rises up. When passion and goodness are held back, darkness rises up. When darkness and goodness are held back, passion rises up. The three qualities take turns being strongest.
Bhagavad Gita 14.10.keyIdea: The three qualities of nature—goodness, passion, and darkness—compete for dominance, and whichever two are suppressed allows the third to emerge.
Bhagavad Gita 14.10.contextNote: This verse describes how the three gunas (qualities of nature) work in constant balance. In the Gita's teaching, all things in nature are made of these three forces, and they shift depending on which ones are held back.

Bhagavad Gita 14.11.simpleEnglish: When knowledge and light spread through all the openings of the body, that is a sign that goodness (sattva) is growing strong.
Bhagavad Gita 14.11.keyIdea: Knowledge spreading through the body shows that the quality of goodness is developing.
Bhagavad Gita 14.11.contextNote: In Gita teaching, sattva is one of three qualities (gunas) that make up all things. When sattva grows, clarity and knowledge increase.

Bhagavad Gita 14.13.simpleEnglish: When darkness (tamas, one of three qualities of nature) grows strong, four things appear: no light, no action, carelessness, and confusion. Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, a descendant of Kuru.
Bhagavad Gita 14.13.keyIdea: Darkness as a force brings passivity, heedlessness, and delusion.
Bhagavad Gita 14.13.contextNote: This verse describes what happens when the quality of darkness increases in a person or situation. It is part of Krishna's teaching about the three qualities (gunas) that shape all nature and behavior.

Bhagavad Gita 14.12.simpleEnglish: When passion grows strong in a person, certain things appear: greed, restless activity, starting many projects, lack of peace, and constant wanting. Krishna is describing what happens inside someone when the passionate quality takes over.
Bhagavad Gita 14.12.keyIdea: Passion (rajas) as a quality of nature produces greed, restlessness, and endless desire.
Bhagavad Gita 14.12.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about the three qualities (gunas) that make up all nature. Rajas, or passion, is one of them. The verse shows what inner state and behavior come with it.

Bhagavad Gita 14.14.simpleEnglish: When a person dies while living in goodness (sattva—a state of clarity, harmony, and virtue), they are reborn in pure worlds where wise people live.
Bhagavad Gita 14.14.keyIdea: A life lived in goodness leads to rebirth in elevated realms.
Bhagavad Gita 14.14.contextNote: This verse describes one outcome of death according to the Gita's teaching on the three qualities (gunas). It reflects the idea that how you live shapes where you are reborn.

Bhagavad Gita 14.15.simpleEnglish: When someone dies while caught up in passion and desire, they are born again among people who are always chasing action and results. When someone dies while caught in darkness and confusion, they are born into ignorant families.
Bhagavad Gita 14.15.keyIdea: The state of mind at death shapes what kind of life you are born into next.
Bhagavad Gita 14.15.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about the three qualities (gunas) that shape all nature and human character. It describes what happens to a person's rebirth based on which quality dominates their mind when they die.

Bhagavad Gita 14.16.simpleEnglish: Good actions bring clean, pure results. Actions driven by passion and desire bring suffering. Actions done in darkness and confusion bring ignorance.
Bhagavad Gita 14.16.keyIdea: The results of actions depend on the quality of mind and intention behind them.
Bhagavad Gita 14.16.contextNote: This verse describes the three gunas (qualities of nature) and how they shape the fruits of our actions. Sattva is clarity and goodness; rajas is passion and restlessness; tamas is darkness and delusion.

Bhagavad Gita 14.17.simpleEnglish: When sattva (the quality of clarity and harmony) is strong, knowledge grows. When rajas (the quality of restless energy) is strong, greed grows. When tamas (the quality of heaviness and confusion) is strong, carelessness, delusion, and ignorance grow.
Bhagavad Gita 14.17.keyIdea: Different qualities of mind produce different kinds of thoughts and behaviors.
Bhagavad Gita 14.17.contextNote: This verse describes how the three gunas (qualities that make up all things) shape what a person thinks and does. It is part of Krishna's teaching about the nature of reality.

Bhagavad Gita 14.18.simpleEnglish: People who live by goodness move upward. People ruled by passion stay in the middle. People caught in darkness and the lowest ways move downward.
Bhagavad Gita 14.18.keyIdea: The Gita teaches that how you live determines where you go—goodness lifts you up, passion keeps you stuck, and darkness pulls you down.
Bhagavad Gita 14.18.contextNote: This verse describes three paths based on the three gunas (qualities): sattva (goodness), rajas (passion/activity), and tamas (darkness/inertia). "Up" and "down" refer to spiritual states or rebirths, not physical movement.

Bhagavad Gita 14.20.simpleEnglish: When a person goes beyond the three qualities (the forces that make up the world and the body), they escape birth, death, aging, and suffering. That person then reaches a state beyond death—immortality.
Bhagavad Gita 14.20.keyIdea: Freedom from the cycle of birth and death comes when you transcend the three qualities that bind the body.
Bhagavad Gita 14.20.contextNote: The "three qualities" (guṇas) are sattva (harmony), rajas (activity), and tamas (inertia)—the forces that create and sustain physical life. This verse teaches that moving beyond their influence leads to liberation.

Bhagavad Gita 14.19.simpleEnglish: When someone sees that only the qualities (the three forces of nature) are doing all the work, and understands that something beyond those qualities exists, that person reaches Krishna's true nature.
Bhagavad Gita 14.19.keyIdea: Understanding that nature's forces do the acting, while something deeper lies beyond them, brings a person to Krishna's essence.
Bhagavad Gita 14.19.contextNote: The "qualities" refer to the three gunas—sattva, rajas, and tamas—the forces that make up the natural world. This verse teaches that when you see through the illusion that *you* are the doer, and recognize a reality beyond nature's forces, you touch something divine.

Bhagavad Gita 14.21.simpleEnglish: Arjuna asks Krishna: What does a person look like who has gone beyond the three qualities (sattva, rajas, and tamas)? How does such a person act? How do they move past these three qualities?
Bhagavad Gita 14.21.keyIdea: Arjuna wants to know the signs and behavior of someone who has transcended the three gunas.
Bhagavad Gita 14.21.contextNote: The three qualities (gunas) are the basic forces that shape all nature and human character in Hindu philosophy. Arjuna is asking what freedom from them looks like.

Bhagavad Gita 14.22.simpleEnglish: A person has moved beyond the three qualities (sattva, rajas, and tamas—the basic forces that shape all things) when they do not hate these qualities when they show up, and do not crave them when they go away. They stay even and calm no matter what.
Bhagavad Gita 14.22.keyIdea: True freedom comes from not being pulled by attraction or repulsion toward the natural forces at work in the world.
Bhagavad Gita 14.22.contextNote: The three qualities—light and clarity, activity and desire, and delusion and heaviness—are always present in nature and in us. This verse teaches that wisdom is not about fighting them, but about staying balanced when they come and go.
