Bhagavad Gita 18.70.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: whoever reads and studies this conversation between us will have made an offering to me through knowledge. That is what I believe.
Bhagavad Gita 18.70.keyIdea: Reading and understanding this teaching is itself a form of worship.
Bhagavad Gita 18.70.contextNote: Krishna is speaking at the end of the Bhagavad Gita. He is saying that the act of learning and reflecting on the dialogue itself has spiritual value.

Bhagavad Gita 18.69.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: no one among people does what pleases me better than this person does. And no one on earth will ever be dearer to me than he is.
Bhagavad Gita 18.69.keyIdea: Krishna is saying that one person stands above all others in devotion and love.
Bhagavad Gita 18.69.contextNote: This verse comes at the end of the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna is speaking about someone who has understood and lived by his teachings. The verse shows how deeply Krishna values those who truly follow his path.

Bhagavad Gita 18.71.simpleEnglish: A person who listens to these teachings with faith and without doubt or criticism will be freed from sin. That person will reach the blessed worlds that come from doing good deeds.
Bhagavad Gita 18.71.keyIdea: Listening to the teachings with faith and an open mind brings freedom and leads to good outcomes.
Bhagavad Gita 18.71.contextNote: This verse closes the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna is saying that even someone who simply listens to these teachings—not just someone who practices them—can benefit spiritually.

Bhagavad Gita 18.73.simpleEnglish: Arjuna says: My confusion is gone. By your grace, I remember who I am. My doubts have left me. I will do what you say.
Bhagavad Gita 18.73.keyIdea: Arjuna has moved from doubt and confusion to clarity and readiness to act.
Bhagavad Gita 18.73.contextNote: This is Arjuna's response after Krishna has finished teaching him. Arjuna is saying that the teaching has resolved his inner conflict.

Bhagavad Gita 18.74.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (a storyteller) says: I heard this conversation between Vasudeva (Krishna) and Arjuna (the high-minded son of Pritha). It was wonderful and made my hair stand on end.
Bhagavad Gita 18.74.keyIdea: Sanjaya is telling someone else about the amazing conversation he witnessed between Krishna and Arjuna.
Bhagavad Gita 18.74.contextNote: This is the final verse of the Bhagavad Gita. Sanjaya is the narrator who has been reporting the entire dialogue to a blind king. He is expressing how powerful and moving the conversation was.

Bhagavad Gita 18.72.simpleEnglish: Krishna asks Arjuna (the warrior Arjuna, also called Dhananjaya) if he has listened carefully with his whole mind focused on one thing. He asks if Arjuna's confusion from not understanding has been cleared away.
Bhagavad Gita 18.72.keyIdea: Krishna checks whether Arjuna has truly understood the teaching and whether his confusion has been resolved.
Bhagavad Gita 18.72.contextNote: This is the final verse of the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna is asking Arjuna to confirm that the long teaching has reached him and worked.

Bhagavad Gita 18.76.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) is speaking to King Dhritarashtra. He says: "O king, every time I remember this amazing and sacred conversation between Krishna (Kesava) and Arjuna, I feel joy again and again."
Bhagavad Gita 18.76.keyIdea: The narrator finds deep joy in recalling the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita.
Bhagavad Gita 18.76.contextNote: Sanjaya has just finished telling the entire Gita to the blind king. This verse shows his own response to what he has witnessed and shared.

Bhagavad Gita 18.75.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) says: I learned this deepest secret—this teaching about devotion—directly from Krishna himself, who is the master of yoga (spiritual practice). I was able to hear it because Vyasa (the ancient poet who wrote the Gita) blessed me with the ability to understand.
Bhagavad Gita 18.75.keyIdea: Sanjaya received the Gita's teachings through Vyasa's grace and Krishna's direct words.
Bhagavad Gita 18.75.contextNote: This verse closes the Bhagavad Gita. Sanjaya is speaking to King Dhritarashtra, explaining how he came to know and tell this sacred conversation between Krishna and Arjuna.

Bhagavad Gita 18.77.simpleEnglish: Sanjaya (the narrator) keeps thinking about the amazing form of Hari (Krishna) that he just saw. Every time he remembers it, he feels wonder and joy all over again.
Bhagavad Gita 18.77.keyIdea: Remembering something sacred can bring back the feeling of awe and happiness each time.
Bhagavad Gita 18.77.contextNote: Sanjaya is describing his own experience after witnessing Krishna's divine form in the previous chapter. This is his personal response to what he saw.

Bhagavad Gita 4.6.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he is unborn and never wears out, and he is the lord of all beings. Yet he still chooses to take control of his own nature and be born in the world through his own power of illusion (maya).
Bhagavad Gita 4.6.keyIdea: Krishna describes how he can be eternal and all-powerful, yet still choose to enter the world and take birth.
Bhagavad Gita 4.6.contextNote: This verse explains a paradox: how can an eternal, unchanging lord be born? Krishna's answer is that his birth is not like ordinary birth—it happens through his own will and power, not through the limits that bind other beings.

Bhagavad Gita 10.23.simpleEnglish: Krishna says he is Shankara (a form of Rudra, the god of storms and destruction) among the Rudras. He is the lord of wealth among the Yakshas and Rakshasas (supernatural beings in Hindu mythology). He is fire among the Vasus (a group of eight deities), and Mount Meru (the highest mountain) among all high mountains.
Bhagavad Gita 10.23.keyIdea: Krishna claims to be the greatest or most important form in many different categories of beings and things.
Bhagavad Gita 10.23.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about his divine nature. He lists examples from Hindu mythology to show that he is present in the most powerful or supreme member of each group.

Bhagavad Gita 16.14.simpleEnglish: A person with a false sense of power says: "I killed this enemy. I will destroy the others too. I am the lord. I enjoy everything. I am perfect, strong, and happy."
Bhagavad Gita 16.14.keyIdea: This verse shows the boastful, arrogant thinking that Krishna will criticize.
Bhagavad Gita 16.14.contextNote: This is the voice of someone caught in ego and delusion about their own power and importance. Krishna is describing this mindset to show what happens when a person forgets that they are not truly in control.

Bhagavad Gita 10.27.simpleEnglish: Krishna says: Among horses, know me as Ucchaiḥśravas (the divine horse born when the gods churned the ocean for nectar). Among great elephants, know me as Airāvata (Indra's white elephant). Among human rulers, know me as the greatest.
Bhagavad Gita 10.27.keyIdea: Krishna is saying that he appears in the most excellent form of each kind of being.
Bhagavad Gita 10.27.contextNote: This verse is part of Krishna's teaching about his divine nature. He lists examples of the finest or most powerful beings in different categories—the best horse, the best elephant, the best human ruler—to show how he manifests in all creation.
